mpi_abort.title: MPI_Abort
mpi_abort.name: MPI_Abort
mpi_abort.summary: Terminate every process in a communicator immediately

params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.errorcode: Status returned to the invoking environment (the shell's exit status, typically).
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_abort.description:
**MPI_Abort** makes a best effort to terminate all processes in **comm**.
 It is the correct way to fail out of a parallel program: a plain STOP on one
 rank leaves the others blocked forever in whatever collective they were
 waiting on, which looks like a hang rather than an error.

 The standard permits aborting only **comm**, but most implementations abort
 the entire job whatever communicator is passed -- do not rely on the narrower
 behaviour.
mpi_abort.result: Does not return. The job terminates with **errorcode**.
mpi_abort.example_code:
if (ios /= 0) then
     write(*,*) 'rank ', rank, ': cannot open input file'
     call MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1, ierr)   ! not STOP
  end if

mpi_allgather.title: MPI_Allgather
mpi_allgather.name: MPI_Allgather
mpi_allgather.summary: Collect data from all processes onto all processes

params.sendcount: Number of elements this process sends.
params.recvbuf: Receive buffer on EVERY process, sized recvcount * nprocs.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_allgather.description:
**MPI_Allgather** is MPI_Gather followed by a broadcast of the result: every
 process ends up with every process's contribution, in rank order. There is no
 root, and every process needs the full-size receive buffer.

 Prefer it to gather-then-broadcast; the implementation has better algorithms
 available than the two calls written out.
mpi_allgather.result: Every process's **recvbuf** holds all contributions in rank order.
mpi_allgather.example_code:
call MPI_Allgather(nlocal, 1, MPI_INTEGER, &
                     counts, 1, MPI_INTEGER, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_allreduce.title: MPI_Allreduce
mpi_allreduce.name: MPI_Allreduce
mpi_allreduce.summary: Combines values from all processes and distributes the result back to all processes

params.sendbuf: Starting address of the send buffer containing `count` elements of type `datatype`. Use MPI_IN_PLACE for in-place operations on intracommunicators.
params.recvbuf: Starting address of the receive buffer where the reduction result will be stored. Must be distinct from `sendbuf` unless using MPI_IN_PLACE.
params.count: Number of elements in `sendbuf` and `recvbuf`. Must be non-negative and identical on all processes.
params.datatype: MPI datatype of elements. Common Fortran types: - MPI_INTEGER, MPI_REAL, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION - MPI_COMPLEX, MPI_DOUBLE_COMPLEX - MPI_LOGICAL, MPI_CHARACTER
params.op: Reduction operation to perform. Predefined operations: - Arithmetic: MPI_SUM, MPI_PROD - Comparison: MPI_MAX, MPI_MIN - Logical: MPI_LAND, MPI_LOR, MPI_LXOR - Bitwise: MPI_BAND, MPI_BOR, MPI_BXOR - Location: MPI_MAXLOC, MPI_MINLOC
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the group of processes participating. Typically MPI_COMM_WORLD for all processes.
params.ierr: Integer error code. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on successful completion.

mpi_allreduce.description: **MPI_Allreduce** performs a global reduction operation (sum, max, min, etc.) on data from all processes in a communicator and distributes the result to all processes. This is equivalent to an MPI_Reduce followed by an MPI_Bcast, but is typically more efficient. All processes contribute data and all processes receive the final result.
mpi_allreduce.result:
On all processes, **recvbuf** contains the combined result of applying
  the reduction operation to the corresponding elements from all processes.
  Unlike MPI_Reduce, every process receives the same result. The operation
  is applied element-wise for arrays (when count > 1). This is equivalent
  to an MPI_Reduce followed by an MPI_Bcast but may be implemented more
  efficiently.
mpi_allreduce.example_code:
program demo_mpi_allreduce
  use mpi
  implicit none
  integer :: ierr, rank, nprocs
  real(8) :: local_sum, global_sum
  real(8) :: local_max, global_max
  real(8) :: local_array(3), global_array(3)

  ! Initialize MPI
  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  ! Example 1: Sum of scalar values across all processes
  local_sum = real(rank + 1, 8)  ! Each process has value rank+1
  call MPI_Allreduce(local_sum, global_sum, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_SUM, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  if (rank == 0) then
    print '(A,F8.2)', 'Global sum: ', global_sum
  end if

  ! Example 2: Maximum value across all processes
  local_max = real(rank * 10, 8)
  call MPI_Allreduce(local_max, global_max, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_MAX, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  if (rank == 0) then
    print '(A,F8.2)', 'Global max: ', global_max
  end if

  ! Example 3: Element-wise reduction of arrays
  local_array = [real(rank, 8), real(rank*2, 8), real(rank*3, 8)]
  call MPI_Allreduce(local_array, global_array, 3, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_SUM, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  if (rank == 0) then
    print '(A,3F8.2)', 'Global array sum: ', global_array
  end if

  ! Example 4: In-place reduction (result overwrites sendbuf)
  local_sum = real(rank + 1, 8)
  call MPI_Allreduce(MPI_IN_PLACE, local_sum, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_SUM, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  if (rank == 0) then
    print '(A,F8.2)', 'In-place sum: ', local_sum
  end if

  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)
end program demo_mpi_allreduce
mpi_allreduce.standard: MPI-1.0 (introduced in the original MPI standard, 1994)

mpi_alltoall.title: MPI_Alltoall
mpi_alltoall.name: MPI_Alltoall
mpi_alltoall.summary: Every process sends a distinct block to every process

params.sendbuf: Blocks to send, one per destination rank, sized sendcount * nprocs.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_alltoall.description:
**MPI_Alltoall** performs a complete exchange: rank i sends its j-th block
 to rank j and receives rank j's i-th block. It is effectively a distributed
 transpose, and the standard step of a parallel FFT.

 Both buffers must hold count * nprocs elements. It moves more data than any
 other collective; on a large job it is usually the scaling bottleneck.
mpi_alltoall.result: Block j of **recvbuf** holds the data rank j sent to this process.
mpi_alltoall.example_code:
call MPI_Alltoall(sbuf, n, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                    rbuf, n, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_any_source.title: MPI_ANY_SOURCE
mpi_any_source.name: MPI_ANY_SOURCE
mpi_any_source.description:
**MPI_ANY_SOURCE** used as the source of a receive matches a message from
 any rank. The actual sender is then read from status(MPI_SOURCE).

 It costs determinism: the order in which messages are taken now depends on
 arrival, so a program using it is not reproducible run to run. That matters
 for anything accumulating floating-point values in receive order. It also
 makes probe-then-receive racy unless the receive names status(MPI_SOURCE)
 rather than the wildcard a second time.
mpi_any_source.example_code:
call MPI_Recv(buf, LPMX, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_ANY_SOURCE, &
                tag, MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)
  call MPI_Get_count(status, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, nrecv, ierr)

mpi_any_tag.title: MPI_ANY_TAG
mpi_any_tag.name: MPI_ANY_TAG
mpi_any_tag.summary: Wildcard: receive a message with any tag
mpi_any_tag.description:
**MPI_ANY_TAG** as the tag of a receive matches a message with any tag; the
 real tag is then status(MPI_TAG).

 As with MPI_ANY_SOURCE it removes ordering guarantees, and it is riskier in
 library code, where it can swallow messages belonging to the application.
 A duplicated communicator (MPI_Comm_dup) is the fix.
mpi_any_tag.example_code:
call MPI_Recv(buf, n, MPI_INTEGER, isrc, MPI_ANY_TAG, &
                MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)
  itag = status(MPI_TAG)

mpi_barrier.title: MPI_Barrier
mpi_barrier.name: MPI_Barrier
mpi_barrier.summary: Block until every process in a communicator has reached this call

params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_barrier.description:
**MPI_Barrier** blocks the calling process until all processes in the
 communicator have called it. It is the only purely synchronizing collective:
 no data moves.

 It is easy to over-use. A barrier is genuinely needed to order operations
 against something outside MPI's knowledge -- writing a shared file, reading a
 wall clock, timing a region -- but MPI's own collectives (MPI_Bcast,
 MPI_Reduce, MPI_Allreduce) already synchronize as much as their semantics
 require, so a barrier placed next to one is usually dead cost.

 A barrier that only SOME processes reach deadlocks the job. That is the usual
 outcome of putting one inside a conditional branch.
mpi_barrier.result:
Returns once every process in **comm** has entered the call. No buffer
  is read or written.
mpi_barrier.example_code:
! Order stdout against the file system, which MPI knows nothing about
  call MPI_Barrier(MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  if (rank == 0) then
     open(unit=10, file='results.dat', status='replace')
     write(10,*) total
     close(10)
  end if
  call MPI_Barrier(MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

  ! Timing a region: without the barrier, t0 measures skew, not work
  call MPI_Barrier(MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  t0 = MPI_Wtime()
  call heavy_work()
  call MPI_Barrier(MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  t1 = MPI_Wtime()

mpi_bcast.title: MPI_Bcast
mpi_bcast.name: MPI_Bcast
mpi_bcast.summary: Broadcast a message from root to all processes in a communicator

params.buffer: Starting address of the data buffer. On the root process, this contains the data to be broadcast. On all other processes, this is where the received data will be stored.
params.count: Number of elements in the buffer. Must be non-negative and identical on all processes.
params.datatype: MPI datatype of each buffer element. Common values include: MPI_INTEGER, MPI_REAL, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_COMPLEX, MPI_LOGICAL, MPI_CHARACTER. Must match on all processes.
params.root: Rank of the process sending the broadcast (0 to comm_size-1). Must be identical on all processes in the communicator.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group. Typically MPI_COMM_WORLD for all processes, or a custom communicator for subgroups.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on successful completion, or an MPI error code on failure.

mpi_bcast.description:
**MPI_Bcast** broadcasts a message from the process with rank **root** to all
 other processes in the group, including itself. After the call, all processes
 in the communicator have identical copies of the buffer data. This is a
 collective operation that must be called by all processes in the communicator.
mpi_bcast.result:
After the call completes, all processes in the communicator have
  identical copies of the data that was in the root process's buffer.
  The buffer on the root process is unchanged; the buffers on all other
  processes contain the broadcast data. This is a collective operation
  that synchronizes all participating processes.
mpi_bcast.example_code:
program demo_mpi_bcast
  use mpi
  implicit none

  integer :: ierr, rank, nprocs
  integer :: root
  real(8) :: value
  real(8), dimension(4) :: array

  ! Initialize MPI
  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  root = 0

  ! Example 1: Broadcast a scalar
  if (rank == root) then
    value = 3.14159265358979d0
    print '(A,I2,A,F12.8)', 'Process ', rank, ' (root) sending value: ', value
  else
    value = 0.0d0
  end if

  call MPI_Bcast(value, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, root, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

  print '(A,I2,A,F12.8)', 'Process ', rank, ' received value: ', value

  ! Example 2: Broadcast an array
  if (rank == root) then
    array = [1.0d0, 2.0d0, 3.0d0, 4.0d0]
    print '(A,I2,A)', 'Process ', rank, ' (root) broadcasting array'
  else
    array = 0.0d0
  end if

  call MPI_Bcast(array, 4, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, root, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

  print '(A,I2,A,4F8.2)', 'Process ', rank, ' array: ', array

  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)
end program demo_mpi_bcast

mpi_byte.title: MPI_BYTE
mpi_byte.name: MPI_BYTE
mpi_byte.summary: Datatype handle for an uninterpreted byte
mpi_byte.description:
**MPI_BYTE** transfers raw bytes with no interpretation and no conversion.

 That last point is the catch: MPI performs representation conversion in a
 heterogeneous job for typed data, and skips it for MPI_BYTE. On a uniform
 cluster it is a convenient way to move a mixed record; across differing
 architectures it corrupts anything but text.
mpi_byte.example_code:
call MPI_Send(record, storage_size(record)/8, MPI_BYTE, &
                dest, 1, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_character.title: MPI_CHARACTER
mpi_character.name: MPI_CHARACTER
mpi_character.description:
**MPI_CHARACTER** is the datatype handle for a single Fortran CHARACTER.
 The count is the number of characters, so a `CHARACTER(LEN=80)` variable is
 sent with count 80, not 1.
mpi_character.example_code:
character(len=80) :: drname
  call MPI_Bcast(drname, 80, MPI_CHARACTER, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_comm_dup.title: MPI_Comm_dup
mpi_comm_dup.name: MPI_Comm_dup

params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_comm_dup.description:
**MPI_Comm_dup** makes a communicator with the same processes and ranks but
 a distinct communication context, so its messages can never match those on
 the original.

 That is what library code needs: a library that communicates on
 MPI_COMM_WORLD can have its messages intercepted by the application's own
 receives, especially where MPI_ANY_TAG is used. Duplicating at initialization
 makes the two message spaces disjoint.
mpi_comm_dup.result: **newcomm** has the same group as **comm** and an isolated message space.
mpi_comm_dup.example_code:
! Give the solver its own message space
  call MPI_Comm_dup(MPI_COMM_WORLD, solver_comm, ierr)

mpi_comm_free.title: MPI_Comm_free
mpi_comm_free.name: MPI_Comm_free

params.comm: The communicator to free. Set to MPI_COMM_NULL on return.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_comm_free.description:
**MPI_Comm_free** marks a communicator for deallocation; it is actually
 released once pending operations on it finish, and the handle is set to
 MPI_COMM_NULL.

 It is collective, so every member must call it. Predefined communicators such
 as MPI_COMM_WORLD must not be freed.
mpi_comm_free.result: The communicator is released and the handle nulled.

mpi_comm_null.title: MPI_COMM_NULL
mpi_comm_null.name: MPI_COMM_NULL
mpi_comm_null.description:
**MPI_COMM_NULL** is the value a communicator handle takes when it names no
 communicator: returned by MPI_Comm_split to a process that passed
 MPI_UNDEFINED as its colour, and left in a handle by MPI_Comm_free.

 Passing it to a communication routine is an error, so a rank excluded by a
 split must be guarded before it uses the result.
mpi_comm_null.example_code:
call MPI_Comm_split(MPI_COMM_WORLD, colour, rank, sub, ierr)
  if (sub /= MPI_COMM_NULL) then
     call MPI_Comm_rank(sub, subrank, ierr)
  end if

mpi_comm_rank.title: MPI_Comm_rank
mpi_comm_rank.name: MPI_Comm_rank
mpi_comm_rank.summary: Get the calling process's rank within a communicator

params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.rank: Returns the calling process's rank, 0 to size-1.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_comm_rank.description:
**MPI_Comm_rank** returns the calling process's index within **comm**,
 counting from ZERO. Together with MPI_Comm_size it is how a process discovers
 which part of the work is its own.

 The rank is meaningful only relative to the communicator it came from. A rank
 obtained from MPI_COMM_WORLD must not be used as a destination in a
 sub-communicator.
mpi_comm_rank.result: **rank** holds the calling process's zero-based index in **comm**.
mpi_comm_rank.example_code:
call MPI_Init(ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  ! Split a loop across ranks
  my_lo = 1 + (rank * n) / nprocs
  my_hi = ((rank + 1) * n) / nprocs

mpi_comm_size.title: MPI_Comm_size
mpi_comm_size.name: MPI_Comm_size
mpi_comm_size.summary: Get the number of processes in a communicator

params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.size: Returns the number of processes in **comm**.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_comm_size.description:
**MPI_Comm_size** returns how many processes belong to **comm**. For
 MPI_COMM_WORLD that is the size of the whole job, as launched by mpirun -n.

 Note the off-by-one that this invites: **size** is a count, but ranks are
 zero-based, so the last rank is size-1.
mpi_comm_size.result: **size** holds the number of processes in the communicator.
mpi_comm_size.example_code:
call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)
  if (rank == nprocs - 1) then     ! NOT nprocs
     print *, 'I am the last rank'
  end if

mpi_comm_split.title: MPI_Comm_split
mpi_comm_split.name: MPI_Comm_split

params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.color: Subgroup selector; equal colours share a communicator. MPI_UNDEFINED to belong to none.
params.key: Controls rank ordering within the new communicator; ties break by rank in **comm**.
params.newcomm: Returns the new communicator, or MPI_COMM_NULL.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_comm_split.description:
**MPI_Comm_split** partitions **comm**: every process supplies a **color**,
 and those sharing a colour end up in the same new communicator, ordered by
 **key**. It is the standard way to build row and column communicators for a
 process grid.

 A process passing MPI_UNDEFINED gets MPI_COMM_NULL and is in no new group --
 useful for excluding ranks, and a source of crashes if the result is then
 used unguarded. Note that ranks in **newcomm** are renumbered from zero.
mpi_comm_split.result: **newcomm** is the caller's new communicator, with ranks numbered afresh.
mpi_comm_split.example_code:
! One communicator per node-row of a 2-D decomposition
  call MPI_Comm_split(MPI_COMM_WORLD, myrow, mycol, row_comm, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(row_comm, row_rank, ierr)     ! renumbered

mpi_comm_world.title: MPI_COMM_WORLD
mpi_comm_world.name: MPI_COMM_WORLD
mpi_comm_world.summary: The communicator containing every process in the job
mpi_comm_world.description:
**MPI_COMM_WORLD** is the predefined communicator holding all processes
 started by the job launcher. It exists from MPI_Init until MPI_Finalize and
 is the default context for nearly all communication.

 Ranks in it run from 0 to size-1 and never change. It cannot be freed. Note
 that a rank number is meaningful only for the communicator it came from --
 a rank taken from MPI_COMM_WORLD is not valid in a communicator produced by
 MPI_Comm_split.
mpi_comm_world.example_code:
call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Bcast(x, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_double_precision.title: MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION
mpi_double_precision.name: MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION
mpi_double_precision.summary: Datatype handle for Fortran DOUBLE PRECISION
mpi_double_precision.description:
**MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION** is the datatype handle matching Fortran
 DOUBLE PRECISION, i.e. REAL*8 / REAL(KIND=8) on every common platform.

 The datatype must match the buffer's actual Fortran type. Passing
 MPI_REAL for a REAL*8 array is not diagnosed by anything -- not the compiler,
 which never sees the connection, and not MPI, which trusts the handle -- and
 transfers half the bytes. Sender and receiver must also agree.
mpi_double_precision.example_code:
real(8) :: x(n)
  call MPI_Bcast(x, n, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_error.title: MPI_ERROR
mpi_error.name: MPI_ERROR
mpi_error.summary: Status array index holding the error code
mpi_error.description:
**MPI_ERROR** indexes a status array at the per-operation error code. It is
 only filled in meaningfully by the multiple-completion calls
 (MPI_Waitall, MPI_Testall and friends), where one request among many may have
 failed; for a single MPI_Recv the code is the routine's own **ierror** and
 this field is not set.
mpi_error.example_code:
call MPI_Waitall(n, reqs, stats, ierr)
  if (ierr /= MPI_SUCCESS) then
     do i = 1, n
        if (stats(MPI_ERROR, i) /= MPI_SUCCESS) call report(i)
     end do
  end if

mpi_f08.title: MPI_F08
mpi_f08.name: MPI_F08
mpi_f08.summary: Modern Fortran MPI bindings module with type-safe interfaces

params.MPI_Comm: Derived type for communicator handles. The predefined communicator MPI_COMM_WORLD is of this type.
params.MPI_Datatype: Derived type for datatype handles. Predefined types include MPI_INTEGER, MPI_REAL, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_COMPLEX, etc.
params.MPI_Status: Derived type for status information returned by receive operations. Contains source, tag, and error fields.
params.MPI_Request: Derived type for nonblocking operation handles.
params.MPI_Op: Derived type for reduction operation handles. Predefined operations include MPI_SUM, MPI_MAX, MPI_MIN, MPI_PROD, etc.

mpi_f08.description:
**mpi_f08** is the recommended MPI module for modern Fortran programs. It
 provides type-safe interfaces using Fortran 2008 features including derived
 types for MPI handles, assumed-type (`TYPE(*)`) for choice buffers, and
 optional error arguments. This module replaces the older `use mpi` and
 `include 'mpif.h'` approaches with improved type safety and better
 compiler error messages.
mpi_f08.result:
After `use mpi_f08`, all MPI routines, constants, and derived types become
  available in the current scope. The module provides the complete MPI
  interface with modern Fortran features.
mpi_f08.example_code:
program demo_mpi_f08
  use mpi_f08
  implicit none
  type(MPI_Comm) :: comm
  type(MPI_Status) :: status
  integer :: rank, nprocs, ierr
  real(8) :: sendbuf, recvbuf

  call MPI_Init(ierr)

  comm = MPI_COMM_WORLD
  call MPI_Comm_rank(comm, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(comm, nprocs, ierr)

  sendbuf = real(rank, 8)

  ! Use MPI_Allreduce with derived type handles
  call MPI_Allreduce(sendbuf, recvbuf, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_SUM, comm, ierr)

  if (rank == 0) then
    print '(A,F8.2)', 'Sum of all ranks: ', recvbuf
  end if

  ! Point-to-point with status
  if (nprocs >= 2) then
    if (rank == 0) then
      call MPI_Send(sendbuf, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 1, 100, comm, ierr)
    else if (rank == 1) then
      call MPI_Recv(recvbuf, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 0, 100, comm, status, ierr)
      print '(A,I0,A,I0)', 'Received from rank ', status%MPI_SOURCE, &
            ' with tag ', status%MPI_TAG
    end if
  end if

  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)

end program demo_mpi_f08

mpi_finalize.title: MPI_Finalize
mpi_finalize.name: MPI_Finalize
mpi_finalize.summary: Shut down the MPI execution environment

params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_finalize.description:
**MPI_Finalize** shuts down the MPI environment and releases its resources.
 Every process that called MPI_Init must call it, and no MPI call other than
 MPI_Initialized and MPI_Finalized is legal afterwards.

 It is not an exit. Execution continues with the next statement, which is why
 rank-0 summary output is usually written after it. It also does not cancel
 outstanding communication: a pending non-blocking request or an unreceived
 message makes the behaviour undefined, so complete or free them first.

 To abort on an error path, use MPI_Abort -- reaching MPI_Finalize requires
 every process to get there, which a failing process by definition will not.
mpi_finalize.result:
Returns after MPI has been shut down. The program continues normally;
  only MPI is unavailable.
mpi_finalize.example_code:
! Normal shutdown
  call MPI_Barrier(MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)

  ! Perfectly legal after finalize -- this is not an exit
  if (rank == 0) print *, 'Total energy: ', etot
  stop

mpi_gather.title: MPI_Gather
mpi_gather.name: MPI_Gather
mpi_gather.summary: Collect data from all processes onto one

params.sendcount: Number of elements this process sends.
params.recvbuf: Receive buffer; significant only on **root**, sized for recvcount * nprocs.
params.recvcount: Elements received from EACH process -- not the total.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_gather.description:
**MPI_Gather** collects an equal-sized block from every process into a
 single array on **root**, ordered by rank.

 The argument that trips everyone: **recvcount** is the number of elements
 received from EACH process, not the total. It is normally equal to
 **sendcount**. The receive buffer must nevertheless be large enough for
 recvcount * nprocs elements, and it need only exist on **root**.

 For unequal block sizes use MPI_Gatherv; for the result on every rank, use
 MPI_Allgather.
mpi_gather.result: On **root**, **recvbuf** holds every process's contribution in rank order.
mpi_gather.example_code:
real(8) :: mine(10), all(10*nprocs)
  call MPI_Gather(mine, 10, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                  all,  10, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_get_count.title: MPI_Get_count
mpi_get_count.name: MPI_Get_count
mpi_get_count.summary: Report how many elements were actually received

params.status: Status array from a completed MPI_Recv, MPI_Probe or MPI_Wait. Declared `INTEGER status(MPI_STATUS_SIZE)` in the Fortran binding.
params.datatype: The datatype the message was received with. Using a different one silently yields a wrong count.
params.count: Number of **datatype** elements received, or MPI_UNDEFINED when the message length is not a whole multiple of the datatype extent.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_get_count.description:
**MPI_Get_count** answers the question MPI_Recv cannot: the count argument
 to MPI_Recv is the buffer CAPACITY, an upper bound, not the size of the
 message that arrived. A shorter message is accepted without complaint, and
 the only way to learn its real length is to ask the status object afterwards.

 Because the answer is expressed in elements of **datatype**, passing a
 different datatype than the receive used gives a wrong -- not an erroneous --
 answer. If the byte count is not an exact multiple of the datatype's extent,
 **count** comes back as MPI_UNDEFINED.
mpi_get_count.result:
**count** holds the number of elements actually received, which may be
  anything from 0 up to the capacity passed to MPI_Recv.
mpi_get_count.example_code:
integer :: status(MPI_STATUS_SIZE), nrecv, ierr
  real(8) :: buf(LPMX)

  ! LPMX is the CAPACITY; the sender may have sent far fewer
  call MPI_Recv(buf, LPMX, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_ANY_SOURCE, &
                tag, MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)
  call MPI_Get_count(status, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, nrecv, ierr)

  ! Only the first nrecv entries are meaningful
  do i = 1, nrecv
     call absorb(buf(i))
  end do

mpi_get_processor_name.title: MPI_Get_processor_name
mpi_get_processor_name.name: MPI_Get_processor_name
mpi_get_processor_name.summary: Get the name of the node this process runs on

params.name: Buffer of at least MPI_MAX_PROCESSOR_NAME characters.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_get_processor_name.description:
**MPI_Get_processor_name** returns an implementation-defined identifier for
 the node -- usually the hostname. Its practical use is confirming process
 placement across nodes.

 Declare **name** with length MPI_MAX_PROCESSOR_NAME and print only
 name(1:resultlen); the rest of the string is unspecified.
mpi_get_processor_name.example_code:
character(len=MPI_MAX_PROCESSOR_NAME) :: nodename
  call MPI_Get_processor_name(nodename, nlen, ierr)
  write(*,*) 'rank ', rank, ' on ', nodename(1:nlen)

mpi_init.title: MPI_Init
mpi_init.name: MPI_Init

params.ierror: Integer error code. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on successful initialization. In the mpi_f08 module, this argument is optional. If omitted and an error occurs, the program will abort.

mpi_init.description:
**MPI_Init** initializes the MPI execution environment. This function must
 be called before any other MPI function (except MPI_Initialized and
 MPI_Get_library_version). It establishes the MPI execution environment,
 including setting up internal data structures, establishing communication
 with other MPI processes, and preparing for message passing operations.
mpi_init.result:
After successful completion, the MPI environment is initialized and ready
  for use. The program can then call MPI_Comm_rank, MPI_Comm_size, and other
  MPI routines. The predefined communicator MPI_COMM_WORLD becomes available,
  containing all processes in the MPI job.
mpi_init.example_code:
program demo_mpi_init
  use mpi_f08
  implicit none
  integer :: rank, nprocs, ierr

  ! Initialize MPI environment
  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  if (ierr /= MPI_SUCCESS) then
    print *, 'Error initializing MPI'
    stop 1
  end if

  ! Get process rank and total number of processes
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  print '(A,I0,A,I0)', 'Hello from process ', rank, ' of ', nprocs

  ! Finalize MPI environment
  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)

end program demo_mpi_init

mpi_init_thread.title: MPI_Init_thread
mpi_init_thread.name: MPI_Init_thread
mpi_init_thread.summary: Initialize MPI with a requested level of thread support

params.provided: Level actually granted -- may be lower than **required**.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_init_thread.description:
**MPI_Init_thread** initializes MPI and negotiates thread support. It is what
 an MPI + OpenMP program must call instead of MPI_Init.

 The critical detail is that **provided** may come back lower than
 **required** and the call still succeeds. Code that asks for
 MPI_THREAD_MULTIPLE and does not check what it got will make concurrent MPI
 calls against an implementation that cannot support them, and fail
 intermittently under load. Check, and degrade deliberately.

 The levels, in increasing order: SINGLE (one thread), FUNNELED (only the
 thread that called this may call MPI), SERIALIZED (any one thread at a time),
 MULTIPLE (unrestricted).
mpi_init_thread.result: MPI is initialized; **provided** states the thread support actually available.
mpi_init_thread.example_code:
call MPI_Init_thread(MPI_THREAD_FUNNELED, provided, ierr)
  if (provided < MPI_THREAD_FUNNELED) then
     write(*,*) 'insufficient MPI thread support'
     call MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1, ierr)
  end if

mpi_integer.title: MPI_INTEGER
mpi_integer.name: MPI_INTEGER
mpi_integer.description:
**MPI_INTEGER** is the datatype handle matching the default Fortran INTEGER.

 It follows the compiler's default integer kind, so a build using
 `-fdefault-integer-8` changes what it must be paired with. Explicit kinds have
 their own handles (MPI_INTEGER4, MPI_INTEGER8).

mpi_iprobe.title: MPI_Iprobe
mpi_iprobe.name: MPI_Iprobe
mpi_iprobe.summary: Check for a message without blocking

params.source: Rank to probe for, or MPI_ANY_SOURCE.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.flag: .TRUE. when a matching message is available.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_iprobe.description:
**MPI_Iprobe** is the non-blocking MPI_Probe: it returns at once, setting
 **flag** to say whether a matching message is waiting. Reading **status**
 when **flag** is .FALSE. gives garbage.

 A tight polling loop on MPI_Iprobe burns a core doing nothing; prefer
 MPI_Probe when there is nothing else to do.
mpi_iprobe.result: **flag** reports availability; **status** describes the message when it is .TRUE.
mpi_iprobe.example_code:
logical :: flag
  call MPI_Iprobe(MPI_ANY_SOURCE, tag, MPI_COMM_WORLD, flag, status, ierr)
  if (flag) then
     call MPI_Get_count(status, MPI_INTEGER, n, ierr)
     call MPI_Recv(ibuf, n, MPI_INTEGER, status(MPI_SOURCE), &
                   status(MPI_TAG), MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)
  end if

mpi_irecv.title: MPI_Irecv
mpi_irecv.name: MPI_Irecv

params.buf: Receive buffer. Do not read until the request completes.
params.count: Buffer CAPACITY in elements -- an upper bound, not the message size.
params.source: Rank to receive from, or MPI_ANY_SOURCE.
params.tag: Message tag to match, or MPI_ANY_TAG.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.request: Returns the handle used to complete the operation.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_irecv.description:
**MPI_Irecv** posts a receive and returns at once. The buffer holds nothing
 useful until MPI_Wait or MPI_Test reports completion, and reading it early is
 the classic non-blocking bug -- it usually appears to work, because the
 message often has arrived.

 Note the missing status: unlike MPI_Recv, there is nowhere here to learn the
 actual source, tag or length. That information comes from the status filled
 in by MPI_Wait, which is what MPI_Get_count must then be given.
mpi_irecv.result: **request** identifies the pending receive; **buf** is not yet valid.
mpi_irecv.example_code:
integer :: req, status(MPI_STATUS_SIZE), nrecv

  call MPI_Irecv(buf, LPMX, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_ANY_SOURCE, &
                 tag, MPI_COMM_WORLD, req, ierr)
  call do_other_work()
  call MPI_Wait(req, status, ierr)              ! status arrives HERE
  call MPI_Get_count(status, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, nrecv, ierr)

mpi_isend.title: MPI_Isend
mpi_isend.name: MPI_Isend

params.buf: Send buffer. Do not modify until the request completes.
params.dest: Rank of the destination process in **comm**.
params.tag: Message tag, matched by the receiver.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.request: Returns the handle used to complete the operation.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_isend.description:
**MPI_Isend** starts a send and returns at once, handing back a **request**
 handle. The send is not finished until MPI_Wait or MPI_Test says it is.

 Two rules make the difference between this and MPI_Send. **buf** may not be
 touched -- read or written -- until completion, because MPI may still be
 reading it; and the request must be completed, or the resources leak and the
 message may never be delivered.

 Its value is overlap: pair MPI_Isend with MPI_Irecv, do interior work, then
 wait. The usual deadlock of two ranks calling MPI_Send to each other
 simultaneously also disappears.
mpi_isend.result: **request** identifies the pending send; the transfer is not complete on return.
mpi_isend.example_code:
call MPI_Irecv(halo_in,  n, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, left,  1, &
                 MPI_COMM_WORLD, req(1), ierr)
  call MPI_Isend(halo_out, n, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, right, 1, &
                 MPI_COMM_WORLD, req(2), ierr)

  call update_interior()          ! overlap with communication

  call MPI_Waitall(2, req, stats, ierr)

mpi_land.title: MPI_LAND
mpi_land.name: MPI_LAND
mpi_land.description:
**MPI_LAND** reduces LOGICAL values with .AND., which is how a global
 convergence test is written: the loop ends only when every rank agrees.

 Use MPI_Allreduce rather than MPI_Reduce for this -- a decision known only to
 the root is not usable as a loop condition, and ranks that leave the loop at
 different iterations deadlock in the next collective.
mpi_land.example_code:
call MPI_Allreduce(done_local, done, 1, MPI_LOGICAL, &
                     MPI_LAND, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  if (done) exit

mpi_logical.title: MPI_LOGICAL
mpi_logical.name: MPI_LOGICAL
mpi_logical.description:
**MPI_LOGICAL** is the datatype handle for Fortran LOGICAL. It pairs with
 the logical reduction operations MPI_LAND, MPI_LOR and MPI_LXOR.

 The bit pattern of .TRUE. is compiler-defined, so a LOGICAL must never be
 sent as MPI_INTEGER between differently built executables.
mpi_logical.example_code:
call MPI_Allreduce(converged_local, converged, 1, MPI_LOGICAL, &
                     MPI_LAND, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_lor.title: MPI_LOR
mpi_lor.name: MPI_LOR
mpi_lor.description:
**MPI_LOR** reduces LOGICAL values with .OR. -- true on every rank when any
 rank contributed true. The natural pairing is a global error flag: any rank
 detecting a problem makes all ranks aware of it, so they can shut down
 together rather than deadlocking.

mpi_max.title: MPI_MAX
mpi_max.name: MPI_MAX
mpi_max.description:
**MPI_MAX** reduces by taking the elementwise maximum. Unlike MPI_SUM it is
 exact and order-independent for floating point, so it reproduces across runs
 and process counts.

 To learn WHICH rank held the maximum, use MPI_MAXLOC with a pair datatype
 such as MPI_2DOUBLE_PRECISION.
mpi_max.example_code:
call MPI_Allreduce(vlocal, vmax, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_MAX, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_maxloc.title: MPI_MAXLOC
mpi_maxloc.name: MPI_MAXLOC
mpi_maxloc.summary: Reduction operation: maximum and its location
mpi_maxloc.description:
**MPI_MAXLOC** returns the maximum together with the rank that held it,
 using a pair datatype exactly as MPI_MINLOC does. Ties resolve to the lowest
 identifier.
mpi_maxloc.example_code:
call MPI_Allreduce(inpair, outpair, 1, MPI_2DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_MAXLOC, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_min.title: MPI_MIN
mpi_min.name: MPI_MIN
mpi_min.description:
**MPI_MIN** reduces by taking the elementwise minimum. Like MPI_MAX it is
 exact and order-independent. Use MPI_MINLOC to also learn which rank held
 the minimum.
mpi_min.example_code:
call MPI_Allreduce(dtlocal, dtmin, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_MIN, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_minloc.title: MPI_MINLOC
mpi_minloc.name: MPI_MINLOC
mpi_minloc.summary: Reduction operation: minimum and its location
mpi_minloc.description:
**MPI_MINLOC** returns both the minimum value and the rank that held it, so
 the buffer is a PAIR type -- MPI_2DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_2INTEGER or
 MPI_2REAL -- and each contribution is two elements: the value followed by an
 integer identifier, conventionally the rank.

 Passing a plain MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION buffer here is a common error; the
 reduction then reads past the value it was given.
mpi_minloc.example_code:
real(8) :: inpair(2), outpair(2)
  inpair(1) = vlocal
  inpair(2) = real(rank, 8)
  call MPI_Allreduce(inpair, outpair, 1, MPI_2DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_MINLOC, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_probe.title: MPI_Probe
mpi_probe.name: MPI_Probe
mpi_probe.summary: Wait for a message and inspect it without receiving

params.source: Rank to probe for, or MPI_ANY_SOURCE.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.status: Describes the pending message: MPI_SOURCE, MPI_TAG and, via MPI_Get_count, its length.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_probe.description:
**MPI_Probe** blocks until a matching message is ready, and fills in
 **status** describing it -- without receiving it. Combined with
 MPI_Get_count, that is how a receiver sizes an allocatable buffer for a
 message whose length it does not know in advance.

 The message stays in the queue, so a matching MPI_Recv must follow. Using
 MPI_ANY_SOURCE in both, without noting status(MPI_SOURCE) and receiving from
 exactly that rank, is a race: a different message may match the receive.
mpi_probe.result: **status** describes a message that is now guaranteed receivable.
mpi_probe.example_code:
call MPI_Probe(MPI_ANY_SOURCE, tag, MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)
  call MPI_Get_count(status, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, n, ierr)
  allocate(buf(n))
  ! receive from THAT rank, not MPI_ANY_SOURCE again
  call MPI_Recv(buf, n, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, status(MPI_SOURCE), &
                status(MPI_TAG), MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)

mpi_prod.title: MPI_PROD
mpi_prod.name: MPI_PROD
mpi_prod.description:
**MPI_PROD** reduces by elementwise multiplication. Like MPI_SUM it is
 order-dependent in floating point, and it overflows far faster -- a product
 over many ranks is usually better computed as a sum of logarithms.
mpi_prod.example_code:
call MPI_Allreduce(plocal, ptotal, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_PROD, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_real.title: MPI_REAL
mpi_real.name: MPI_REAL
mpi_real.description:
**MPI_REAL** is the datatype handle for the default Fortran REAL, i.e.
 single precision.

 The most damaging datatype mistake in Fortran MPI is using it for a REAL*8
 array. Nothing diagnoses it: the compiler cannot see the association and MPI
 trusts the handle. Half the bytes move and the data is silently wrong. For
 REAL*8 the handle is MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION.
mpi_real.example_code:
real :: x(n)                                  ! single precision
  call MPI_Bcast(x, n, MPI_REAL, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_recv.title: MPI_Recv
mpi_recv.name: MPI_Recv

params.buf: Starting address of the receive buffer with room for count elements. The received data is stored starting at this address.
params.count: Maximum number of elements to receive. The actual message may be shorter but not longer than this count.
params.datatype: MPI datatype handle describing each buffer element.
params.source: Rank of the sending process within comm, or MPI_ANY_SOURCE to receive from any process. MPI_PROC_NULL is allowed for a null receive.
params.tag: Message tag for matching, or MPI_ANY_TAG to match any tag.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group.
params.status: Status object that receives information about the message: status%MPI_SOURCE contains the source rank, status%MPI_TAG contains the tag, and MPI_Get_count can determine the message length.
params.ierror: Error code. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on successful completion.

mpi_recv.description:
**MPI_Recv** performs a standard-mode blocking receive operation. It blocks
 until the receive buffer contains the newly received message from the
 specified source. The actual length of the received message can be
 determined using MPI_Get_count on the returned status. The received
 message length must be less than or equal to the buffer length specified
 by count; otherwise, an MPI_ERR_TRUNCATE error occurs.
mpi_recv.result:
The receive buffer is filled with data from the matching send operation.
  The status object contains metadata about the received message including
  the actual source rank and tag used.
mpi_recv.example_code:
program demo_mpi_recv
  use mpi_f08
  implicit none
  integer :: rank, nprocs, ierr
  real(8) :: data(100)
  type(MPI_Status) :: status
  integer :: recv_count, i

  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  if (nprocs < 2) then
    print *, 'This example requires at least 2 processes'
    call MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1, ierr)
  end if

  if (rank == 0) then
    ! Send 50 elements to process 1
    data(1:50) = [(real(i, 8), i = 1, 50)]
    call MPI_Send(data, 50, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 1, 99, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
    print *, 'Process 0 sent 50 elements'
  else if (rank == 1) then
    ! Receive into buffer with room for 100 elements
    call MPI_Recv(data, 100, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 0, 99, &
                  MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)

    ! Query actual received count
    call MPI_Get_count(status, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, recv_count, ierr)

    print '(A,I0)', 'Process 1 received elements: ', recv_count
    print '(A,I0)', 'Source rank: ', status%MPI_SOURCE
    print '(A,I0)', 'Message tag: ', status%MPI_TAG
    print '(A,5F6.1)', 'First 5 values: ', data(1:5)
  end if

  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)

end program demo_mpi_recv

mpi_reduce.title: MPI_Reduce
mpi_reduce.name: MPI_Reduce
mpi_reduce.summary: Perform a global reduction operation across all processes in a communicator

params.sendbuf: Address of the send buffer containing count elements of the specified datatype. Each process contributes its local data to the reduction. The root process may use MPI_IN_PLACE to use recvbuf as both input and output.
params.recvbuf: Address of the receive buffer where the reduction result is stored. Only significant at the root process; ignored on other processes.
params.count: Number of elements in the send buffer. Must be non-negative and identical across all processes in the communicator.
params.datatype: MPI datatype handle describing each element. Common values: MPI_INTEGER, MPI_REAL, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_COMPLEX, MPI_LOGICAL.
params.op: MPI reduction operation handle. Predefined operations: - MPI_MAX - Maximum value - MPI_MIN - Minimum value - MPI_SUM - Sum - MPI_PROD - Product - MPI_LAND - Logical AND - MPI_BAND - Bitwise AND - MPI_LOR - Logical OR - MPI_BOR - Bitwise OR - MPI_LXOR - Logical XOR - MPI_BXOR - Bitwise XOR - MPI_MAXLOC - Maximum value and location - MPI_MINLOC - Minimum value and location
params.root: Rank of the root process (0 to size-1) within the communicator. Only this process receives the reduction result in recvbuf.
params.comm: MPI communicator handle defining the process group. Typically MPI_COMM_WORLD for all processes or a user-defined communicator.
params.ierr: Integer error code. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure.

mpi_reduce.description:
**MPI_Reduce** combines the elements provided in the input buffer of each
 process in the group, using the specified reduction operation **op**, and
 returns the combined value in the output buffer of the process with rank
 **root**. The operation is performed element-wise when count > 1.
mpi_reduce.result:
On the root process, **recvbuf** contains the combined result of applying
  the reduction operation to the corresponding elements from all processes.
  The operation is applied element-wise for arrays (when count > 1). The
  recvbuf on non-root processes is not modified and may contain undefined
  values. For MPI_MAXLOC and MPI_MINLOC operations, the result includes
  both the extreme value and the rank of the process that contributed it.
mpi_reduce.example_code:
program demo_mpi_reduce
  use mpi
  implicit none

  integer :: ierr, rank, nprocs
  real(8) :: local_value, global_sum, global_max, global_min
  real(8), dimension(3) :: local_array, sum_array
  integer :: i

  ! Initialize MPI
  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  ! Each process has a different value based on its rank
  local_value = real(rank + 1, 8) * 10.0d0

  ! Reduce with SUM operation - result goes to root (rank 0)
  call MPI_Reduce(local_value, global_sum, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                  MPI_SUM, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

  ! Reduce with MAX operation
  call MPI_Reduce(local_value, global_max, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                  MPI_MAX, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

  ! Reduce with MIN operation
  call MPI_Reduce(local_value, global_min, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                  MPI_MIN, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

  ! Only root process has valid results
  if (rank == 0) then
    print '(A,I0,A)', 'Running with ', nprocs, ' processes'
    print '(A,F10.2)', 'Global sum: ', global_sum
    print '(A,F10.2)', 'Global max: ', global_max
    print '(A,F10.2)', 'Global min: ', global_min
  end if

  ! Example with arrays: reduce multiple elements at once
  do i = 1, 3
    local_array(i) = real(rank * 3 + i, 8)
  end do

  call MPI_Reduce(local_array, sum_array, 3, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                  MPI_SUM, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

  if (rank == 0) then
    print '(A)', 'Array reduction (SUM):'
    print '(A,3F8.2)', '  Result: ', sum_array
  end if

  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)

end program demo_mpi_reduce

mpi_request_null.title: MPI_REQUEST_NULL
mpi_request_null.name: MPI_REQUEST_NULL
mpi_request_null.description:
**MPI_REQUEST_NULL** is the value MPI_Wait and friends leave in a request
 handle once the operation has completed.

 It is useful deliberately: waiting on a null request returns at once with an
 empty status, so an array of requests can be pre-filled with it and passed to
 MPI_Waitall even when only some entries were actually posted.
mpi_request_null.example_code:
req = MPI_REQUEST_NULL
  if (has_left)  call MPI_Irecv(l, n, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, left, 1, &
                                MPI_COMM_WORLD, req(1), ierr)
  call MPI_Waitall(2, req, stats, ierr)   ! unposted entries are fine

mpi_scan.title: MPI_Scan
mpi_scan.name: MPI_Scan

params.recvbuf: Returns the prefix reduction over ranks 0..this rank.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_scan.description:
**MPI_Scan** gives rank i the reduction of the contributions of ranks 0
 through i inclusive. With MPI_SUM it is the classic way to turn per-rank
 counts into global offsets -- each rank learns where its own block starts in
 a concatenated array.

 Note the inclusive semantics: for an offset you usually want the sum of the
 ranks BEFORE you, which is MPI_Exscan, or MPI_Scan's result minus your own
 contribution.
mpi_scan.result: **recvbuf** holds the reduction over ranks 0 through the caller's rank.
mpi_scan.example_code:
call MPI_Scan(nlocal, nupto, 1, MPI_INTEGER, MPI_SUM, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  my_offset = nupto - nlocal        ! exclusive prefix

mpi_scatter.title: MPI_Scatter
mpi_scatter.name: MPI_Scatter
mpi_scatter.summary: Distribute distinct blocks from one process to all

params.sendbuf: Data to distribute; significant only on **root**.
params.sendcount: Elements sent to EACH process -- not the total.
params.root: Rank holding the data to distribute.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group, typically MPI_COMM_WORLD.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_scatter.description:
**MPI_Scatter** splits an array on **root** into equal blocks and sends the
 i-th block to rank i. It is the exact inverse of MPI_Gather, and shares its
 trap: **sendcount** is per-destination, not the size of the whole array.

 Contrast MPI_Bcast, which gives every process the SAME data; scatter gives
 each a different piece.
mpi_scatter.result: Each process's **recvbuf** holds its own block of **sendbuf**.
mpi_scatter.example_code:
real(8) :: whole(10*nprocs), mine(10)
  call MPI_Scatter(whole, 10, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                   mine,  10, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_send.title: MPI_Send
mpi_send.name: MPI_Send

params.buf: Starting address of the send buffer containing count elements of the specified datatype. The buffer contents are transmitted to the destination.
params.count: Number of elements to send. Must be non-negative. A count of 0 sends an empty message.
params.datatype: MPI datatype handle describing each buffer element. Common types: MPI_INTEGER, MPI_REAL, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_COMPLEX, MPI_LOGICAL.
params.dest: Rank of destination process within comm (0 to comm_size-1). MPI_PROC_NULL is allowed for a null send (no operation).
params.tag: Message tag for matching with a corresponding receive. Must be non-negative and less than MPI_TAG_UB.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group.
params.ierror: Error code. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on successful completion.

mpi_send.description:
**MPI_Send** performs a standard-mode blocking send operation. It transmits
 count elements of the specified datatype from the send buffer to the
 destination process. The call blocks until the send buffer can be safely
 reused by the caller, which may occur before, during, or after the
 matching receive completes, depending on the MPI implementation's
 buffering behavior.
mpi_send.result:
The send buffer data is transmitted to the destination process. The call
  returns when the buffer can be safely reused; this does not guarantee
  the message has been received. Use MPI_Ssend for synchronous behavior
  or MPI_Bsend for buffered sends.
mpi_send.example_code:
program demo_mpi_send
  use mpi_f08
  implicit none
  integer :: rank, nprocs, ierr
  real(8) :: message(10)
  type(MPI_Status) :: status
  integer :: i

  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  if (nprocs < 2) then
    print *, 'This example requires at least 2 processes'
    call MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1, ierr)
  end if

  if (rank == 0) then
    ! Process 0 sends data to process 1
    message = [(real(i, 8), i = 1, 10)]
    print *, 'Process 0 sending:', message(1:5), '...'
    call MPI_Send(message, 10, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 1, 42, &
                  MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
    print *, 'Process 0 send completed'
  else if (rank == 1) then
    ! Process 1 receives data from process 0
    call MPI_Recv(message, 10, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 0, 42, &
                  MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)
    print *, 'Process 1 received:', message(1:5), '...'
  end if

  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)

end program demo_mpi_send

mpi_sendrecv.title: MPI_Sendrecv
mpi_sendrecv.name: MPI_Sendrecv

params.sendbuf: Starting address of the send buffer containing sendcount elements of type sendtype to be sent to the destination process.
params.sendcount: Number of elements to send. Must be non-negative.
params.sendtype: MPI datatype of each send buffer element.
params.dest: Rank of destination process within comm. Can be MPI_PROC_NULL for no send.
params.sendtag: Message tag for the send operation. Must be non-negative.
params.recvbuf: Starting address of the receive buffer with room for recvcount elements.
params.recvcount: Maximum number of elements to receive.
params.recvtype: MPI datatype of each receive buffer element.
params.source: Rank of source process, or MPI_ANY_SOURCE to receive from any process.
params.recvtag: Message tag for matching, or MPI_ANY_TAG to match any tag.
params.comm: MPI communicator for the operation.
params.status: Status object containing source rank, tag, and message size information.
params.ierror: Error code. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success.

mpi_sendrecv.description:
**MPI_Sendrecv** executes a blocking send and receive operation in a single
 call. It sends data from sendbuf to the destination process and receives
 data into recvbuf from the source process. This routine is useful for
 avoiding deadlocks that can occur with separate send and receive calls,
 particularly in ring or shift communication patterns.
mpi_sendrecv.result:
The send buffer data is transmitted to the destination process and the
  receive buffer is filled with data from the source process. The status
  object contains information about the received message including the
  actual source rank and tag.
mpi_sendrecv.example_code:
program demo_mpi_sendrecv
  use mpi_f08
  implicit none
  integer :: rank, nprocs, ierr
  integer :: left, right
  real(8) :: sendbuf, recvbuf
  type(MPI_Status) :: status

  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  ! Set up ring topology
  left = mod(rank - 1 + nprocs, nprocs)
  right = mod(rank + 1, nprocs)

  ! Each process sends its rank to the right neighbor
  ! and receives from the left neighbor
  sendbuf = real(rank, 8)

  call MPI_Sendrecv(sendbuf, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, right, 100, &
                    recvbuf, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, left, 100, &
                    MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)

  print '(A,I0,A,F4.1,A,I0)', 'Rank ', rank, ' received ', recvbuf, &
        ' from rank ', status%MPI_SOURCE

  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)

end program demo_mpi_sendrecv

mpi_source.title: MPI_SOURCE
mpi_source.name: MPI_SOURCE
mpi_source.summary: Status array index holding the sender's rank
mpi_source.description:
**MPI_SOURCE** is the index into a status array at which the sending rank is
 stored. It is how a receive posted with MPI_ANY_SOURCE discovers who actually
 sent the message.

 It is an INDEX, not the rank itself: the value wanted is
 `status(MPI_SOURCE)`. Using MPI_SOURCE directly as a rank is a real and
 quiet bug, since it is a small integer and will often name a valid process.
mpi_source.example_code:
call MPI_Recv(buf, n, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_ANY_SOURCE, &
                tag, MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)
  isender = status(MPI_SOURCE)          ! not MPI_SOURCE

mpi_status_size.title: MPI_STATUS_SIZE
mpi_status_size.name: MPI_STATUS_SIZE
mpi_status_size.summary: Length of the Fortran status array
mpi_status_size.description:
**MPI_STATUS_SIZE** is the extent of the INTEGER array that holds an MPI
 status in the Fortran binding. Every status variable is declared with it:

     INTEGER status(MPI_STATUS_SIZE)

 and an array of statuses, for MPI_Waitall, is
 `INTEGER stats(MPI_STATUS_SIZE, n)` -- that order, which is easy to reverse.

 The array's fields are reached by the named indices MPI_SOURCE, MPI_TAG and
 MPI_ERROR; the remaining entries are opaque, and the received length is
 obtained through MPI_Get_count rather than by indexing.
mpi_status_size.example_code:
integer :: status(MPI_STATUS_SIZE)
  call MPI_Recv(buf, n, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_ANY_SOURCE, &
                tag, MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)
  src = status(MPI_SOURCE)

mpi_success.title: MPI_SUCCESS
mpi_success.name: MPI_SUCCESS
mpi_success.description:
**MPI_SUCCESS** is the value (zero) returned in **ierror** when a call
 succeeds.

 Testing it is nearly always pointless: MPI's default error handler on
 MPI_COMM_WORLD aborts the job rather than returning, so a failing call does
 not come back at all. The check becomes meaningful only after
 MPI_Comm_set_errhandler installs MPI_ERRORS_RETURN.

mpi_sum.title: MPI_SUM
mpi_sum.name: MPI_SUM
mpi_sum.description:
**MPI_SUM** is the predefined reduction operation adding contributions
 elementwise, for MPI_Reduce, MPI_Allreduce and MPI_Scan.

 Floating-point addition is not associative, so the result depends on the
 order the implementation chose -- which may differ between runs, and between
 process counts, even on identical input. A reduction that must be
 bit-reproducible needs a fixed-order reduction written by hand.
mpi_sum.example_code:
call MPI_Allreduce(elocal, etotal, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_SUM, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

mpi_tag.title: MPI_TAG
mpi_tag.name: MPI_TAG
mpi_tag.summary: Status array index holding the message tag
mpi_tag.description:
**MPI_TAG** indexes a status array at the position holding the tag of the
 received message -- the counterpart of MPI_SOURCE, and the way a receive
 posted with MPI_ANY_TAG learns what actually arrived. It is an index, not the
 tag itself.
mpi_tag.example_code:
call MPI_Recv(buf, n, MPI_INTEGER, MPI_ANY_SOURCE, MPI_ANY_TAG, &
                MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)
  itag = status(MPI_TAG)

mpi_type_commit.title: MPI_Type_commit
mpi_type_commit.name: MPI_Type_commit

params.datatype: The derived type to commit, from MPI_Type_contiguous or similar.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_type_commit.description:
**MPI_Type_commit** finalizes a derived datatype so it can be used in
 communication calls. Using an uncommitted type is an error, and it is the
 usual reason a freshly constructed datatype fails.

 Only derived types need it -- MPI_INTEGER and friends are already usable.
mpi_type_commit.example_code:
call MPI_Type_contiguous(3, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, xyz_type, ierr)
  call MPI_Type_commit(xyz_type, ierr)

mpi_type_contiguous.title: MPI_Type_contiguous
mpi_type_contiguous.name: MPI_Type_contiguous
mpi_type_contiguous.summary: Define a datatype of contiguous elements

params.count: Number of **oldtype** elements in the new type.
params.newtype: Returns the new datatype handle, uncommitted.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_type_contiguous.description:
**MPI_Type_contiguous** builds a datatype describing **count** consecutive
 **oldtype** elements -- the simplest derived type, useful for sending
 fixed-size records as one unit rather than counting elements everywhere.

 The handle is not usable until MPI_Type_commit has been called on it, and
 leaks unless MPI_Type_free is called eventually.
mpi_type_contiguous.result: **newtype** is a handle that must be committed before use.
mpi_type_contiguous.example_code:
call MPI_Type_contiguous(3, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, xyz_type, ierr)
  call MPI_Type_commit(xyz_type, ierr)
  call MPI_Send(pos, natoms, xyz_type, dest, 1, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  call MPI_Type_free(xyz_type, ierr)

mpi_type_free.title: MPI_Type_free
mpi_type_free.name: MPI_Type_free

params.datatype: The derived type to free. Set to MPI_DATATYPE_NULL on return.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_type_free.description:
**MPI_Type_free** releases a derived datatype and sets the handle to
 MPI_DATATYPE_NULL. Types derived FROM it stay valid, as does any
 communication already in progress.

 Freeing types matters in code that builds them inside a loop; a long run can
 otherwise exhaust the implementation's handle table.
mpi_type_free.result: The handle is released and set to MPI_DATATYPE_NULL.

mpi_undefined.title: MPI_UNDEFINED
mpi_undefined.name: MPI_UNDEFINED
mpi_undefined.description:
**MPI_UNDEFINED** marks a value that does not exist. Two places matter: as
 the colour argument to MPI_Comm_split it excludes the process, which then
 receives MPI_COMM_NULL; and MPI_Get_count returns it when the message length
 is not a whole multiple of the datatype's extent.

 The second is worth checking for -- an unchecked MPI_UNDEFINED count is a
 large negative number and will be used as a loop bound.
mpi_undefined.example_code:
call MPI_Get_count(status, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, n, ierr)
  if (n == MPI_UNDEFINED) call MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 2, ierr)

mpi_wait.title: MPI_Wait
mpi_wait.name: MPI_Wait
mpi_wait.summary: Block until a non-blocking operation completes

params.request: The handle from MPI_Isend/MPI_Irecv. Set to MPI_REQUEST_NULL on return.
params.status: Status of the completed operation. For a receive this is where MPI_SOURCE, MPI_TAG and the length come from.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_wait.description:
**MPI_Wait** blocks until the operation identified by **request** finishes,
 then frees the request and sets it to MPI_REQUEST_NULL.

 For a receive, **status** is where the actual source, tag and length finally
 become available -- MPI_Irecv had nowhere to put them. For a send it carries
 little of interest.

 Waiting on an already-null request returns immediately with an empty status,
 which is what makes it safe to wait over an array of requests where only some
 were posted.
mpi_wait.result: Returns once the operation is complete; **request** is freed.
mpi_wait.example_code:
call MPI_Wait(req, status, ierr)
  src = status(MPI_SOURCE)
  call MPI_Get_count(status, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, nrecv, ierr)

mpi_waitall.title: MPI_Waitall
mpi_waitall.name: MPI_Waitall
mpi_waitall.summary: Block until all of a set of operations complete

params.count: Number of requests in the array.
params.array_of_requests: Requests to complete; all set to MPI_REQUEST_NULL on return.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure. In the Fortran binding this is a mandatory final argument -- omitting it is the single most common Fortran MPI bug, and the compiler cannot catch it.

mpi_waitall.description:
**MPI_Waitall** completes a whole array of requests. Prefer it to a loop of
 MPI_Wait calls: waiting on request 1 first forces that particular ordering,
 while MPI_Waitall lets the implementation take them as they arrive.

 The status array is two-dimensional in Fortran -- INTEGER statuses
 (MPI_STATUS_SIZE, count) -- which is easy to declare the wrong way round.
mpi_waitall.result: Returns once every request has completed.
mpi_waitall.example_code:
integer :: req(2), stats(MPI_STATUS_SIZE, 2)

  call MPI_Irecv(rbuf, n, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, left,  9, MPI_COMM_WORLD, req(1), ierr)
  call MPI_Isend(sbuf, n, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, right, 9, MPI_COMM_WORLD, req(2), ierr)
  call MPI_Waitall(2, req, stats, ierr)

mpi_wtime.title: MPI_Wtime
mpi_wtime.name: MPI_Wtime
mpi_wtime.description:
**MPI_Wtime** returns wall-clock seconds from an unspecified origin, so
 only differences between two calls mean anything.

 Two things spoil a measurement. The clocks are per-process by default, so
 differences taken across ranks are not comparable; and without a barrier
 before the first call the timing includes whatever skew the ranks arrived
 with. Bracket the region with MPI_Barrier to measure the region rather than
 the imbalance.

 Being a function with no arguments, it must be declared DOUBLE PRECISION when
 IMPLICIT NONE is in force and mpif.h is used.
mpi_wtime.result: Wall-clock seconds as DOUBLE PRECISION, measured from an arbitrary origin.
mpi_wtime.example_code:
double precision :: t0, t1

  call MPI_Barrier(MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  t0 = MPI_Wtime()
  call compute_forces()
  call MPI_Barrier(MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  t1 = MPI_Wtime()

  if (rank == 0) print *, 'forces: ', t1 - t0, ' s'

mpiallreduce.title: MPI_Allreduce
mpiallreduce.name: MPI_Allreduce
mpiallreduce.summary: Combines values from all processes and distributes the result back to all processes

params.sendbuf: Starting address of the send buffer containing `count` elements of type `datatype`. Use MPI_IN_PLACE for in-place operations on intracommunicators.
params.recvbuf: Starting address of the receive buffer where the reduction result will be stored. Must be distinct from `sendbuf` unless using MPI_IN_PLACE.
params.count: Number of elements in `sendbuf` and `recvbuf`. Must be non-negative and identical on all processes.
params.datatype: MPI datatype of elements. Common Fortran types: - MPI_INTEGER, MPI_REAL, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION - MPI_COMPLEX, MPI_DOUBLE_COMPLEX - MPI_LOGICAL, MPI_CHARACTER
params.op: Reduction operation to perform. Predefined operations: - Arithmetic: MPI_SUM, MPI_PROD - Comparison: MPI_MAX, MPI_MIN - Logical: MPI_LAND, MPI_LOR, MPI_LXOR - Bitwise: MPI_BAND, MPI_BOR, MPI_BXOR - Location: MPI_MAXLOC, MPI_MINLOC
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the group of processes participating. Typically MPI_COMM_WORLD for all processes.
params.ierr: Integer error code. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on successful completion.

mpiallreduce.description: **MPI_Allreduce** performs a global reduction operation (sum, max, min, etc.) on data from all processes in a communicator and distributes the result to all processes. This is equivalent to an MPI_Reduce followed by an MPI_Bcast, but is typically more efficient. All processes contribute data and all processes receive the final result.
mpiallreduce.result:
On all processes, **recvbuf** contains the combined result of applying
  the reduction operation to the corresponding elements from all processes.
  Unlike MPI_Reduce, every process receives the same result. The operation
  is applied element-wise for arrays (when count > 1). This is equivalent
  to an MPI_Reduce followed by an MPI_Bcast but may be implemented more
  efficiently.
mpiallreduce.example_code:
program demo_mpi_allreduce
  use mpi
  implicit none
  integer :: ierr, rank, nprocs
  real(8) :: local_sum, global_sum
  real(8) :: local_max, global_max
  real(8) :: local_array(3), global_array(3)

  ! Initialize MPI
  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  ! Example 1: Sum of scalar values across all processes
  local_sum = real(rank + 1, 8)  ! Each process has value rank+1
  call MPI_Allreduce(local_sum, global_sum, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_SUM, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  if (rank == 0) then
    print '(A,F8.2)', 'Global sum: ', global_sum
  end if

  ! Example 2: Maximum value across all processes
  local_max = real(rank * 10, 8)
  call MPI_Allreduce(local_max, global_max, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_MAX, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  if (rank == 0) then
    print '(A,F8.2)', 'Global max: ', global_max
  end if

  ! Example 3: Element-wise reduction of arrays
  local_array = [real(rank, 8), real(rank*2, 8), real(rank*3, 8)]
  call MPI_Allreduce(local_array, global_array, 3, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_SUM, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  if (rank == 0) then
    print '(A,3F8.2)', 'Global array sum: ', global_array
  end if

  ! Example 4: In-place reduction (result overwrites sendbuf)
  local_sum = real(rank + 1, 8)
  call MPI_Allreduce(MPI_IN_PLACE, local_sum, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                     MPI_SUM, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
  if (rank == 0) then
    print '(A,F8.2)', 'In-place sum: ', local_sum
  end if

  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)
end program demo_mpi_allreduce
mpiallreduce.standard: MPI-1.0 (introduced in the original MPI standard, 1994)

mpibcast.title: MPI_Bcast
mpibcast.name: MPI_Bcast
mpibcast.summary: Broadcast a message from root to all processes in a communicator

params.buffer: Starting address of the data buffer. On the root process, this contains the data to be broadcast. On all other processes, this is where the received data will be stored.
params.count: Number of elements in the buffer. Must be non-negative and identical on all processes.
params.datatype: MPI datatype of each buffer element. Common values include: MPI_INTEGER, MPI_REAL, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_COMPLEX, MPI_LOGICAL, MPI_CHARACTER. Must match on all processes.
params.root: Rank of the process sending the broadcast (0 to comm_size-1). Must be identical on all processes in the communicator.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group. Typically MPI_COMM_WORLD for all processes, or a custom communicator for subgroups.
params.ierror: Error status. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on successful completion, or an MPI error code on failure.

mpibcast.description:
**MPI_Bcast** broadcasts a message from the process with rank **root** to all
 other processes in the group, including itself. After the call, all processes
 in the communicator have identical copies of the buffer data. This is a
 collective operation that must be called by all processes in the communicator.
mpibcast.result:
After the call completes, all processes in the communicator have
  identical copies of the data that was in the root process's buffer.
  The buffer on the root process is unchanged; the buffers on all other
  processes contain the broadcast data. This is a collective operation
  that synchronizes all participating processes.
mpibcast.example_code:
program demo_mpi_bcast
  use mpi
  implicit none

  integer :: ierr, rank, nprocs
  integer :: root
  real(8) :: value
  real(8), dimension(4) :: array

  ! Initialize MPI
  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  root = 0

  ! Example 1: Broadcast a scalar
  if (rank == root) then
    value = 3.14159265358979d0
    print '(A,I2,A,F12.8)', 'Process ', rank, ' (root) sending value: ', value
  else
    value = 0.0d0
  end if

  call MPI_Bcast(value, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, root, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

  print '(A,I2,A,F12.8)', 'Process ', rank, ' received value: ', value

  ! Example 2: Broadcast an array
  if (rank == root) then
    array = [1.0d0, 2.0d0, 3.0d0, 4.0d0]
    print '(A,I2,A)', 'Process ', rank, ' (root) broadcasting array'
  else
    array = 0.0d0
  end if

  call MPI_Bcast(array, 4, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, root, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

  print '(A,I2,A,4F8.2)', 'Process ', rank, ' array: ', array

  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)
end program demo_mpi_bcast

mpiinit.title: MPI_Init
mpiinit.name: MPI_Init

params.ierror: Integer error code. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on successful initialization. In the mpi_f08 module, this argument is optional. If omitted and an error occurs, the program will abort.

mpiinit.description:
**MPI_Init** initializes the MPI execution environment. This function must
 be called before any other MPI function (except MPI_Initialized and
 MPI_Get_library_version). It establishes the MPI execution environment,
 including setting up internal data structures, establishing communication
 with other MPI processes, and preparing for message passing operations.
mpiinit.result:
After successful completion, the MPI environment is initialized and ready
  for use. The program can then call MPI_Comm_rank, MPI_Comm_size, and other
  MPI routines. The predefined communicator MPI_COMM_WORLD becomes available,
  containing all processes in the MPI job.
mpiinit.example_code:
program demo_mpi_init
  use mpi_f08
  implicit none
  integer :: rank, nprocs, ierr

  ! Initialize MPI environment
  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  if (ierr /= MPI_SUCCESS) then
    print *, 'Error initializing MPI'
    stop 1
  end if

  ! Get process rank and total number of processes
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  print '(A,I0,A,I0)', 'Hello from process ', rank, ' of ', nprocs

  ! Finalize MPI environment
  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)

end program demo_mpi_init

mpirecv.title: MPI_Recv
mpirecv.name: MPI_Recv

params.buf: Starting address of the receive buffer with room for count elements. The received data is stored starting at this address.
params.count: Maximum number of elements to receive. The actual message may be shorter but not longer than this count.
params.datatype: MPI datatype handle describing each buffer element.
params.source: Rank of the sending process within comm, or MPI_ANY_SOURCE to receive from any process. MPI_PROC_NULL is allowed for a null receive.
params.tag: Message tag for matching, or MPI_ANY_TAG to match any tag.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group.
params.status: Status object that receives information about the message: status%MPI_SOURCE contains the source rank, status%MPI_TAG contains the tag, and MPI_Get_count can determine the message length.
params.ierror: Error code. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on successful completion.

mpirecv.description:
**MPI_Recv** performs a standard-mode blocking receive operation. It blocks
 until the receive buffer contains the newly received message from the
 specified source. The actual length of the received message can be
 determined using MPI_Get_count on the returned status. The received
 message length must be less than or equal to the buffer length specified
 by count; otherwise, an MPI_ERR_TRUNCATE error occurs.
mpirecv.result:
