The receive buffer is filled with data from the matching send operation.
  The status object contains metadata about the received message including
  the actual source rank and tag used.
mpirecv.example_code:
program demo_mpi_recv
  use mpi_f08
  implicit none
  integer :: rank, nprocs, ierr
  real(8) :: data(100)
  type(MPI_Status) :: status
  integer :: recv_count, i

  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  if (nprocs < 2) then
    print *, 'This example requires at least 2 processes'
    call MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1, ierr)
  end if

  if (rank == 0) then
    ! Send 50 elements to process 1
    data(1:50) = [(real(i, 8), i = 1, 50)]
    call MPI_Send(data, 50, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 1, 99, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
    print *, 'Process 0 sent 50 elements'
  else if (rank == 1) then
    ! Receive into buffer with room for 100 elements
    call MPI_Recv(data, 100, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 0, 99, &
                  MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)

    ! Query actual received count
    call MPI_Get_count(status, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, recv_count, ierr)

    print '(A,I0)', 'Process 1 received elements: ', recv_count
    print '(A,I0)', 'Source rank: ', status%MPI_SOURCE
    print '(A,I0)', 'Message tag: ', status%MPI_TAG
    print '(A,5F6.1)', 'First 5 values: ', data(1:5)
  end if

  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)

end program demo_mpi_recv

mpireduce.title: MPI_Reduce
mpireduce.name: MPI_Reduce
mpireduce.summary: Perform a global reduction operation across all processes in a communicator

params.sendbuf: Address of the send buffer containing count elements of the specified datatype. Each process contributes its local data to the reduction. The root process may use MPI_IN_PLACE to use recvbuf as both input and output.
params.recvbuf: Address of the receive buffer where the reduction result is stored. Only significant at the root process; ignored on other processes.
params.count: Number of elements in the send buffer. Must be non-negative and identical across all processes in the communicator.
params.datatype: MPI datatype handle describing each element. Common values: MPI_INTEGER, MPI_REAL, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_COMPLEX, MPI_LOGICAL.
params.op: MPI reduction operation handle. Predefined operations: - MPI_MAX - Maximum value - MPI_MIN - Minimum value - MPI_SUM - Sum - MPI_PROD - Product - MPI_LAND - Logical AND - MPI_BAND - Bitwise AND - MPI_LOR - Logical OR - MPI_BOR - Bitwise OR - MPI_LXOR - Logical XOR - MPI_BXOR - Bitwise XOR - MPI_MAXLOC - Maximum value and location - MPI_MINLOC - Minimum value and location
params.root: Rank of the root process (0 to size-1) within the communicator. Only this process receives the reduction result in recvbuf.
params.comm: MPI communicator handle defining the process group. Typically MPI_COMM_WORLD for all processes or a user-defined communicator.
params.ierr: Integer error code. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success, or an MPI error code on failure.

mpireduce.description:
**MPI_Reduce** combines the elements provided in the input buffer of each
 process in the group, using the specified reduction operation **op**, and
 returns the combined value in the output buffer of the process with rank
 **root**. The operation is performed element-wise when count > 1.
mpireduce.result:
On the root process, **recvbuf** contains the combined result of applying
  the reduction operation to the corresponding elements from all processes.
  The operation is applied element-wise for arrays (when count > 1). The
  recvbuf on non-root processes is not modified and may contain undefined
  values. For MPI_MAXLOC and MPI_MINLOC operations, the result includes
  both the extreme value and the rank of the process that contributed it.
mpireduce.example_code:
program demo_mpi_reduce
  use mpi
  implicit none

  integer :: ierr, rank, nprocs
  real(8) :: local_value, global_sum, global_max, global_min
  real(8), dimension(3) :: local_array, sum_array
  integer :: i

  ! Initialize MPI
  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  ! Each process has a different value based on its rank
  local_value = real(rank + 1, 8) * 10.0d0

  ! Reduce with SUM operation - result goes to root (rank 0)
  call MPI_Reduce(local_value, global_sum, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                  MPI_SUM, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

  ! Reduce with MAX operation
  call MPI_Reduce(local_value, global_max, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                  MPI_MAX, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

  ! Reduce with MIN operation
  call MPI_Reduce(local_value, global_min, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                  MPI_MIN, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

  ! Only root process has valid results
  if (rank == 0) then
    print '(A,I0,A)', 'Running with ', nprocs, ' processes'
    print '(A,F10.2)', 'Global sum: ', global_sum
    print '(A,F10.2)', 'Global max: ', global_max
    print '(A,F10.2)', 'Global min: ', global_min
  end if

  ! Example with arrays: reduce multiple elements at once
  do i = 1, 3
    local_array(i) = real(rank * 3 + i, 8)
  end do

  call MPI_Reduce(local_array, sum_array, 3, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, &
                  MPI_SUM, 0, MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)

  if (rank == 0) then
    print '(A)', 'Array reduction (SUM):'
    print '(A,3F8.2)', '  Result: ', sum_array
  end if

  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)

end program demo_mpi_reduce

mpisend.title: MPI_Send
mpisend.name: MPI_Send

params.buf: Starting address of the send buffer containing count elements of the specified datatype. The buffer contents are transmitted to the destination.
params.count: Number of elements to send. Must be non-negative. A count of 0 sends an empty message.
params.datatype: MPI datatype handle describing each buffer element. Common types: MPI_INTEGER, MPI_REAL, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, MPI_COMPLEX, MPI_LOGICAL.
params.dest: Rank of destination process within comm (0 to comm_size-1). MPI_PROC_NULL is allowed for a null send (no operation).
params.tag: Message tag for matching with a corresponding receive. Must be non-negative and less than MPI_TAG_UB.
params.comm: MPI communicator defining the process group.
params.ierror: Error code. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on successful completion.

mpisend.description:
**MPI_Send** performs a standard-mode blocking send operation. It transmits
 count elements of the specified datatype from the send buffer to the
 destination process. The call blocks until the send buffer can be safely
 reused by the caller, which may occur before, during, or after the
 matching receive completes, depending on the MPI implementation's
 buffering behavior.
mpisend.result:
The send buffer data is transmitted to the destination process. The call
  returns when the buffer can be safely reused; this does not guarantee
  the message has been received. Use MPI_Ssend for synchronous behavior
  or MPI_Bsend for buffered sends.
mpisend.example_code:
program demo_mpi_send
  use mpi_f08
  implicit none
  integer :: rank, nprocs, ierr
  real(8) :: message(10)
  type(MPI_Status) :: status
  integer :: i

  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  if (nprocs < 2) then
    print *, 'This example requires at least 2 processes'
    call MPI_Abort(MPI_COMM_WORLD, 1, ierr)
  end if

  if (rank == 0) then
    ! Process 0 sends data to process 1
    message = [(real(i, 8), i = 1, 10)]
    print *, 'Process 0 sending:', message(1:5), '...'
    call MPI_Send(message, 10, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 1, 42, &
                  MPI_COMM_WORLD, ierr)
    print *, 'Process 0 send completed'
  else if (rank == 1) then
    ! Process 1 receives data from process 0
    call MPI_Recv(message, 10, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, 0, 42, &
                  MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)
    print *, 'Process 1 received:', message(1:5), '...'
  end if

  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)

end program demo_mpi_send

mpisendrecv.title: MPI_Sendrecv
mpisendrecv.name: MPI_Sendrecv

params.sendbuf: Starting address of the send buffer containing sendcount elements of type sendtype to be sent to the destination process.
params.sendcount: Number of elements to send. Must be non-negative.
params.sendtype: MPI datatype of each send buffer element.
params.dest: Rank of destination process within comm. Can be MPI_PROC_NULL for no send.
params.sendtag: Message tag for the send operation. Must be non-negative.
params.recvbuf: Starting address of the receive buffer with room for recvcount elements.
params.recvcount: Maximum number of elements to receive.
params.recvtype: MPI datatype of each receive buffer element.
params.source: Rank of source process, or MPI_ANY_SOURCE to receive from any process.
params.recvtag: Message tag for matching, or MPI_ANY_TAG to match any tag.
params.comm: MPI communicator for the operation.
params.status: Status object containing source rank, tag, and message size information.
params.ierror: Error code. Returns MPI_SUCCESS (0) on success.

mpisendrecv.description:
**MPI_Sendrecv** executes a blocking send and receive operation in a single
 call. It sends data from sendbuf to the destination process and receives
 data into recvbuf from the source process. This routine is useful for
 avoiding deadlocks that can occur with separate send and receive calls,
 particularly in ring or shift communication patterns.
mpisendrecv.result:
The send buffer data is transmitted to the destination process and the
  receive buffer is filled with data from the source process. The status
  object contains information about the received message including the
  actual source rank and tag.
mpisendrecv.example_code:
program demo_mpi_sendrecv
  use mpi_f08
  implicit none
  integer :: rank, nprocs, ierr
  integer :: left, right
  real(8) :: sendbuf, recvbuf
  type(MPI_Status) :: status

  call MPI_Init(ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_rank(MPI_COMM_WORLD, rank, ierr)
  call MPI_Comm_size(MPI_COMM_WORLD, nprocs, ierr)

  ! Set up ring topology
  left = mod(rank - 1 + nprocs, nprocs)
  right = mod(rank + 1, nprocs)

  ! Each process sends its rank to the right neighbor
  ! and receives from the left neighbor
  sendbuf = real(rank, 8)

  call MPI_Sendrecv(sendbuf, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, right, 100, &
                    recvbuf, 1, MPI_DOUBLE_PRECISION, left, 100, &
                    MPI_COMM_WORLD, status, ierr)

  print '(A,I0,A,F4.1,A,I0)', 'Rank ', rank, ' received ', recvbuf, &
        ' from rank ', status%MPI_SOURCE

  call MPI_Finalize(ierr)

end program demo_mpi_sendrecv

omp barrier.title: barrier
omp barrier.name: barrier
omp barrier.description:
**barrier** specifies an explicit synchronization point at which all threads in the current team must wait. When a thread reaches the barrier directive, it halts execution until all other threads in the team have also reached the barrier. Once all threads arrive and complete any pending explicit tasks bound to the parallel region, they resume parallel execution of subsequent code.

 The barrier construct ensures that all work performed by threads before the barrier is visible to all threads after the barrier. This is essential for maintaining data consistency when threads need to share results from parallel computations.

### **Options**\n\nNone. This is a stand-alone synchronization construct that accepts no clauses or arguments.
omp barrier.result: When all threads have reached the barrier, the synchronization is complete. All memory operations performed before the barrier by any thread are guaranteed to be visible to all threads after the barrier. Execution resumes with all threads synchronized at the same point in the program. The barrier establishes a happens-before relationship between code preceding and following the barrier across all threads.
omp barrier.example_code:
program demo_omp_barrier
  use omp_lib
  implicit none
  integer :: thread_id
  integer, parameter :: n = 4
  integer :: partial_sums(n)
  integer :: total_sum
  integer :: i

  total_sum = 0

  !$omp parallel num_threads(n) private(thread_id) shared(partial_sums, total_sum)
    thread_id = omp_get_thread_num()

    ! Each thread computes its partial sum
    partial_sums(thread_id + 1) = (thread_id + 1) * 10
    print '(A,I0,A,I0)', 'Thread ', thread_id, ' computed partial sum: ', partial_sums(thread_id + 1)

    ! Wait for all threads to finish computing
    !$omp barrier

    ! Only thread 0 computes the total after all partial sums are ready
    !$omp single
      do i = 1, n
        total_sum = total_sum + partial_sums(i)
      end do
      print '(A,I0)', 'Total sum after barrier: ', total_sum
    !$omp end single
  !$omp end parallel

end program demo_omp_barrier

omp_atomic.title: omp_atomic
omp_atomic.name: omp_atomic
omp_atomic.summary: !$OMP ATOMIC - atomic update of a single memory location
omp_atomic.description:
**ATOMIC** makes one update to one memory location indivisible. It is far
 cheaper than `critical` because it maps to a hardware atomic instruction, but
 it is correspondingly narrow: exactly one scalar update, of a restricted
 form, and the expression on the right is NOT evaluated atomically.

 Use `critical` when more than one location must change together.
omp_atomic.example_code:
!$omp atomic
  count = count + 1

  !$omp atomic capture          ! atomically take the old value
  old = idx
  idx = idx + 1
  !$omp end atomic

omp_barrier.title: omp_barrier_directive
omp_barrier.name: omp_barrier_directive
omp_barrier.summary: !$OMP BARRIER - synchronize all threads in a team
omp_barrier.description:
**BARRIER** blocks every thread of the team until all have arrived.

 It must be reached by ALL threads: placing one inside a conditional, or
 inside a `single` or `master` block, deadlocks the program. That is the
 commonest way to hang an OpenMP code.

 Most of the time it is unnecessary -- `do`, `single` and `sections` already
 carry an implicit barrier at their end unless `nowait` removes it.
omp_barrier.example_code:
!$omp parallel
  call phase_one()
  !$omp barrier            ! every thread reaches this
  call phase_two()
  !$omp end parallel

omp_collapse.title: collapse(n)
omp_collapse.name: collapse(n)
omp_collapse.summary: Fuse nested loops into one iteration space
omp_collapse.description:
**collapse** merges the given number of perfectly nested loops into a single
 iteration space before distributing it. It matters when the outer loop is
 shorter than the thread count -- with 32 threads and an outer loop of 4,
 parallelizing the outer loop alone leaves 28 threads idle.

 The loops must be PERFECTLY nested: no statements between them, and the inner
 bounds must not depend on the outer index. A triangular loop
 (`do j = i, n`) cannot be collapsed.

 Collapsing can also destroy memory locality, since the fused iteration order
 no longer follows Fortran's column-major layout as directly. Measure it.
omp_collapse.example_code:
!$omp parallel do collapse(2) private(i, j)
  do k = 1, 4                     ! too short to parallelize alone
     do j = 1, n
        c(j,k) = a(j,k) + b(j,k)
     end do
  end do

omp_copyin.title: copyin(list)
omp_copyin.name: copyin(list)
omp_copyin.summary: Initialize threadprivate copies from the master's values
omp_copyin.description:
**copyin** initializes each thread's `threadprivate` copy from the master
 thread's value at the start of the region.

 Without it, the non-master copies are undefined on entry to the first
 parallel region -- which is the trap when threading legacy Fortran, where a
 COMMON block was filled by a setup routine and every thread is expected to
 see it.
omp_copyin.example_code:
common /work/ params(20)
  !$omp threadprivate(/work/)
  call read_params()             ! master fills it
  !$omp parallel copyin(/work/)
  call uses_params()             ! every thread sees it
  !$omp end parallel

omp_copyprivate.title: copyprivate(list)
omp_copyprivate.name: copyprivate(list)
omp_copyprivate.summary: Broadcast one thread's values to the rest of the team
omp_copyprivate.description:
**copyprivate** takes the values the executing thread of a `single`
 construct produced and broadcasts them to every other thread's copies. It is
 how a value read or computed once gets distributed without a shared variable
 and a barrier.

 It appears only on `end single`, and cannot be combined with `nowait` -- the
 broadcast needs the barrier it would remove.
omp_copyprivate.example_code:
!$omp parallel private(nsteps)
  !$omp single
  read(5,*) nsteps
  !$omp end single copyprivate(nsteps)
  call run(nsteps)               ! every thread has it
  !$omp end parallel

omp_critical.title: omp_critical
omp_critical.name: omp_critical
omp_critical.summary: !$OMP CRITICAL - mutual exclusion for a block
omp_critical.description:
**CRITICAL** admits one thread at a time to the enclosed block.

 Unnamed critical regions all share ONE name. Two unrelated unnamed critical
 sections in different subroutines therefore exclude each other, which is a
 silent serialization bug in code that looks correct -- name them.

 For a single scalar update, `atomic` is much cheaper; for accumulating into a
 variable across a loop, a `reduction` clause is cheaper still and clearer.
omp_critical.example_code:
!$omp parallel do
  do i = 1, n
     e = energy(i)
     !$omp critical (etot_update)
     total = total + e
     !$omp end critical (etot_update)
  end do

  ! better still -- no lock at all
  !$omp parallel do reduction(+:total)
  do i = 1, n
     total = total + energy(i)
  end do

omp_default.title: default(none | shared | private)
omp_default.name: default(none | shared | private)
omp_default.summary: Set the data-sharing rule for variables not named explicitly
omp_default.directive: !$omp parallel do default(none) shared(a) private(i, tmp)
omp_default.description:
**default** controls how variables not named in another clause are treated.

 `default(none)` is worth adopting as a habit. It requires every variable in
 the region to be classified explicitly, turning the commonest OpenMP bug -- a
 scratch variable left shared -- from a silent race into a compile error. The
 cost is verbosity; the benefit is that the compiler finds the race instead of
 a user.

 `default(shared)` is the implicit behaviour. `default(private)` is a Fortran
 extension and not available in C/C++.
omp_default.example_code:
!$omp parallel do default(none) shared(a, b, n) private(i, tmp)
  do i = 1, n
     tmp = a(i) * a(i)
     b(i) = tmp
  end do

omp_destroy_lock.title: omp_destroy_lock
omp_destroy_lock.name: omp_destroy_lock
omp_destroy_lock.summary: Release the resources of an OpenMP lock

params.svar: The lock variable to destroy; must be unlocked.

omp_destroy_lock.description:
**omp_destroy_lock** deallocates a lock's resources. The lock must be
 initialized and unlocked; destroying a held lock is undefined.

omp_destroy_nest_lock.title: omp_destroy_nest_lock
omp_destroy_nest_lock.name: omp_destroy_nest_lock
omp_destroy_nest_lock.summary: Release the resources of a nestable OpenMP lock

params.nvar: The nestable lock variable to destroy.

omp_destroy_nest_lock.description:
**omp_destroy_nest_lock** deallocates a nestable lock's resources. It must
 be initialized and unlocked.

omp_firstprivate.title: firstprivate(list)
omp_firstprivate.name: firstprivate(list)
omp_firstprivate.summary: Private copies initialized from the value before the region
omp_firstprivate.description:
**firstprivate** is `private` whose copies are initialized with the value
 the variable held on entry. It is the clause meant whenever a private
 variable is read before it is written.

 The initialization happens ONCE per thread, not once per iteration, so a
 variable modified inside the loop carries its change into that thread's later
 iterations. When each iteration must start afresh, assign it explicitly.

 It is also the default for most variables inside a `task`, which is a
 different default from a parallel region and a common source of confusion.
omp_firstprivate.example_code:
scale = 2.5d0
  !$omp parallel do firstprivate(scale)
  do i = 1, n
     b(i) = scale * a(i)          ! scale is 2.5 in every thread
  end do

omp_flush.title: omp_flush
omp_flush.name: omp_flush
omp_flush.summary: !$OMP FLUSH - make a thread's view of memory consistent
omp_flush.description:
**FLUSH** forces a consistent view of the listed variables (or of all
 shared variables) between a thread and memory.

 It is rarely written by hand: `barrier`, `critical`, `atomic` and the ends of
 worksharing constructs all flush implicitly. Explicit flushes are for
 hand-rolled synchronization, which is very hard to get right -- a flush
 orders memory but does NOT prevent two threads reaching the same point at
 once.
omp_flush.example_code:
!$omp flush(ready)
  do while (.not. ready)
     !$omp flush(ready)
  end do

omp_get_active_level.title: omp_get_active_level
omp_get_active_level.name: omp_get_active_level
omp_get_active_level.summary: Get the number of nested ACTIVE parallel regions
omp_get_active_level.description:
**omp_get_active_level** counts only regions executing with more than one
 thread, where omp_get_level counts every enclosing region. The two differ
 wherever a region was collapsed to a single thread by an `if` clause or by
 dynamic adjustment.
omp_get_active_level.result: Number of enclosing active parallel regions.

omp_get_ancestor_thread_num.title: omp_get_ancestor_thread_num
omp_get_ancestor_thread_num.name: omp_get_ancestor_thread_num
omp_get_ancestor_thread_num.summary: Get this thread's ancestor id at a given nesting level

params.level: Nesting level to query, from 0 to omp_get_level().

omp_get_ancestor_thread_num.description:
**omp_get_ancestor_thread_num** returns the thread number, at nesting
 **level**, of the ancestor of the calling thread. At the caller's own level it
 is omp_get_thread_num(); at level 0 it is 0. Out-of-range levels give -1.
omp_get_ancestor_thread_num.result: The ancestor's thread number, or -1 for an invalid level.

omp_get_dynamic.title: omp_get_dynamic
omp_get_dynamic.name: omp_get_dynamic
omp_get_dynamic.summary: Test whether dynamic thread adjustment is enabled
omp_get_dynamic.description:
**omp_get_dynamic** reports whether the runtime may reduce team sizes below
 the requested number.

omp_get_level.title: omp_get_level
omp_get_level.name: omp_get_level
omp_get_level.summary: Get the number of nested parallel regions enclosing the caller
omp_get_level.description:
**omp_get_level** returns how many nested parallel regions enclose the
 caller: 0 in serial code, 1 in a simple parallel region, and more when
 nesting is enabled. It counts regions whether or not they are active.
omp_get_level.result: Nesting depth of parallel regions; 0 in serial code.

omp_get_max_active_levels.title: omp_get_max_active_levels
omp_get_max_active_levels.name: omp_get_max_active_levels
omp_get_max_active_levels.summary: Get the maximum depth of active nested parallelism
omp_get_max_active_levels.description:
**omp_get_max_active_levels** returns the current limit on the depth of
 active nested parallel regions. A value of 1 means nested regions run
 serially.

omp_get_max_threads.title: omp_get_max_threads
omp_get_max_threads.name: omp_get_max_threads
omp_get_max_threads.summary: Get the thread count a new parallel region would use
omp_get_max_threads.description:
**omp_get_max_threads** returns how many threads the next parallel region
 would start with, given the current settings. Unlike omp_get_num_threads it is
 meaningful in serial code, which makes it the right call for sizing per-thread
 arrays before entering a region.

 It is an upper bound, not a promise: a num_threads clause or dynamic
 adjustment can still produce a smaller team.
omp_get_max_threads.result: The thread count a parallel region would use if started now.
omp_get_max_threads.example_code:
nt = omp_get_max_threads()
  allocate(partial(nt))
  !$omp parallel
  partial(omp_get_thread_num()+1) = local_work()
  !$omp end parallel

omp_get_nested.title: omp_get_nested
omp_get_nested.name: omp_get_nested
omp_get_nested.summary: Test whether nested parallelism is enabled (deprecated)
omp_get_nested.description:
**omp_get_nested** reports whether nested parallelism is enabled.
 Deprecated in OpenMP 5.0; use omp_get_max_active_levels instead.

omp_get_num_procs.title: omp_get_num_procs
omp_get_num_procs.name: omp_get_num_procs
omp_get_num_procs.summary: Get the number of processors available
omp_get_num_procs.description:
**omp_get_num_procs** returns the number of processors available to the
 program.

 On a shared cluster node this is routinely wrong for the job: it reports what
 the OS sees, which is the whole node, not the cores the batch scheduler
 allocated. Sizing a thread team from it on a shared node oversubscribes the
 machine. Prefer OMP_NUM_THREADS as set by the job script.
omp_get_num_procs.result: The number of processors available to the program.
omp_get_num_procs.example_code:
! Diagnostic only -- do NOT size the team from this on a shared node
  if (omp_get_thread_num() == 0) print *, 'cores visible: ', omp_get_num_procs()

omp_get_num_threads.title: omp_get_num_threads
omp_get_num_threads.name: omp_get_num_threads
omp_get_num_threads.summary: Get the number of threads in the current team
omp_get_num_threads.description:
**omp_get_num_threads** returns the size of the team executing the current
 parallel region.

 Called OUTSIDE a parallel region it returns 1 -- it reports the current team,
 not the number that would be used. The value that a future region will use is
 omp_get_max_threads(), and confusing the two is why a diagnostic print before
 a parallel region reports a single thread.
omp_get_num_threads.result: The number of threads in the current team; 1 in serial code.
omp_get_num_threads.example_code:
print *, omp_get_num_threads()   ! 1 -- serial region
  print *, omp_get_max_threads()   ! what a parallel region would use

  !$omp parallel
  !$omp master
  print *, omp_get_num_threads()   ! the real team size
  !$omp end master
  !$omp end parallel

omp_get_schedule.title: omp_get_schedule
omp_get_schedule.name: omp_get_schedule
omp_get_schedule.summary: Get the schedule used by `schedule(runtime)` loops
omp_get_schedule.description:
**omp_get_schedule** returns the schedule and chunk size that
 `schedule(runtime)` loops currently use.
omp_get_schedule.result: **kind** and **chunk_size** describe the current runtime schedule.

omp_get_team_size.title: omp_get_team_size
omp_get_team_size.name: omp_get_team_size
omp_get_team_size.summary: Get the team size at a given nesting level

params.level: Nesting level to query, from 0 to omp_get_level().

omp_get_team_size.description:
**omp_get_team_size** returns the number of threads in the team to which
 the caller's ancestor at **level** belonged. Level 0 gives 1; out-of-range
 levels give -1.
omp_get_team_size.result: The team size at that level, or -1 for an invalid level.

omp_get_thread_limit.title: omp_get_thread_limit
omp_get_thread_limit.name: omp_get_thread_limit
omp_get_thread_limit.summary: Get the maximum number of threads available to the program
omp_get_thread_limit.description:
**omp_get_thread_limit** returns the ceiling on threads for the whole
 program, as set by OMP_THREAD_LIMIT. It bounds the total across all nested
 teams, where omp_get_max_threads bounds one team.
omp_get_thread_limit.result: The program-wide maximum number of threads.

omp_get_thread_num.title: omp_get_thread_num
omp_get_thread_num.name: omp_get_thread_num
omp_get_thread_num.summary: Get the calling thread's number within its team
omp_get_thread_num.description:
**omp_get_thread_num** returns the calling thread's id within its current
 team, from 0 to omp_get_num_threads()-1. The master thread is 0.

 The number is per-TEAM, not global: inside nested parallel regions two
 different threads can both be thread 0. Outside any parallel region it
 returns 0, which is why a serial call looks like it worked.

 A thread number is not a stable identity for scheduling work -- with dynamic
 scheduling the mapping of iterations to threads changes between runs.
omp_get_thread_num.result: The calling thread's id, 0 to omp_get_num_threads()-1.
omp_get_thread_num.example_code:
!$omp parallel private(tid)
  tid = omp_get_thread_num()
  if (tid == 0) print *, 'threads: ', omp_get_num_threads()
  !$omp end parallel

omp_get_wtick.title: omp_get_wtick
omp_get_wtick.name: omp_get_wtick
omp_get_wtick.description:
**omp_get_wtick** returns the number of seconds between successive ticks of
 the omp_get_wtime clock -- its resolution. A measured interval close to this
 value is noise.

omp_get_wtime.title: omp_get_wtime
omp_get_wtime.name: omp_get_wtime
omp_get_wtime.description:
**omp_get_wtime** returns wall-clock seconds from an arbitrary origin; only
 differences are meaningful. It is the OpenMP counterpart of MPI_Wtime.

 Times taken by different threads are comparable only if
 OMP_GET_WTIME_IS_GLOBAL-style consistency holds; measure on one thread when
 in doubt. Note it measures ELAPSED time, so a parallel region that halves the
 wall time still consumes about the same CPU time.
omp_get_wtime.result: Wall-clock seconds as DOUBLE PRECISION, from an arbitrary origin.
omp_get_wtime.example_code:
t0 = omp_get_wtime()
  !$omp parallel do
  do i = 1, n
     call work(i)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do
  print *, 'elapsed: ', omp_get_wtime() - t0

omp_if.title: if(scalar-logical-expr)
omp_if.name: if(scalar-logical-expr)
omp_if.summary: Parallelize only when a condition holds
omp_if.description:
**if** makes the region parallel only when the expression is true; otherwise
 it executes on one thread.

 It exists because starting a thread team costs real time -- typically a few
 microseconds -- which a short loop cannot repay. A loop that is sometimes
 large and sometimes tiny, called in an inner routine, can be slower in
 parallel than in serial, and this clause is how that is expressed without
 duplicating the loop.

 The region still exists when the condition is false, so data-sharing clauses
 apply and `omp_in_parallel()` returns .FALSE.
omp_if.example_code:
!$omp parallel do if(n > 1000) private(i)
  do i = 1, n
     a(i) = a(i) * 2.0d0
  end do

omp_in_parallel.title: omp_in_parallel
omp_in_parallel.name: omp_in_parallel
omp_in_parallel.summary: Test whether the caller is inside an active parallel region
omp_in_parallel.description:
**omp_in_parallel** returns .TRUE. when called from within an active
 parallel region. It lets a routine behave correctly whether called from serial
 or parallel context -- for example, taking a lock only when it is actually
 needed.

 An active region with one thread still counts as parallel; a region disabled
 by an `if` clause does not.
omp_in_parallel.result: .TRUE. inside an active parallel region, .FALSE. otherwise.
omp_in_parallel.example_code:
if (omp_in_parallel()) then
     !$omp critical
     call append_to_log(msg)
     !$omp end critical
  else
     call append_to_log(msg)
  end if

omp_init_lock.title: omp_init_lock
omp_init_lock.name: omp_init_lock
omp_init_lock.description:
**omp_init_lock** initializes a lock variable and leaves it unlocked. It
 must be called before any other lock routine touches the variable, and must
 not be called on an already-initialized lock.

 Initialize from serial code: two threads initializing the same lock race.
omp_init_lock.result: The lock is initialized and unlocked.
omp_init_lock.example_code:
integer(kind=omp_lock_kind) :: lck
  call omp_init_lock(lck)        ! serial region

omp_init_nest_lock.title: omp_init_nest_lock
omp_init_nest_lock.name: omp_init_nest_lock
omp_init_nest_lock.description:
**omp_init_nest_lock** initializes a nestable lock -- one the owning thread
 may acquire repeatedly, releasing it as many times as it took it. Use it where
 a locked region can call code that takes the same lock; a simple lock
 deadlocks there.
omp_init_nest_lock.result: The nestable lock is initialized and unlocked.

omp_lastprivate.title: lastprivate(list)
omp_lastprivate.name: lastprivate(list)
omp_lastprivate.summary: Private copies, with the sequentially-last value copied out
omp_lastprivate.description:
**lastprivate** is `private` whose value from the SEQUENTIALLY last
 iteration -- the one the serial loop would have run last -- is copied back to
 the original after the region.

 "Sequentially last" is the important part: it is not whichever thread
 finished last, so the result is deterministic regardless of scheduling.

 Copies are still uninitialized on entry; combine with `firstprivate` on the
 same variable if the incoming value is also needed.
omp_lastprivate.example_code:
!$omp parallel do lastprivate(tmp)
  do i = 1, n
     tmp = a(i) * b(i)
  end do
  ! tmp now holds the value from i = n

omp_lib.title: omp_lib
omp_lib.name: omp_lib
omp_lib.description:
**omp_lib** declares the OpenMP runtime routines, their kind parameters
 (`omp_lock_kind`, `omp_nest_lock_kind`, `omp_sched_kind`) and the schedule
 constants. `USE omp_lib` is the modern spelling; the older
 `INCLUDE 'omp_lib.h'` exists for fixed-form code that predates modules.

 It is only declarations. The directives themselves need no module -- but they
 DO need the compiler flag: without `-fopenmp` (gfortran) or `-qopenmp`
 (Intel), every `!$OMP` line is an ordinary comment, the code compiles
 cleanly, and it runs on one thread. A program can therefore be "working" and
 entirely serial. This config passes `-fopenmp` when linting so a malformed
 directive is reported rather than ignored.

 The conditional-compilation sentinel `!$` is subject to the same flag: those
 lines become live Fortran under OpenMP and stay comments without it, which is
 the usual way to guard a call to omp_get_thread_num in code that must also
 build serially.
omp_lib.example_code:
program demo
  use omp_lib
  implicit none
  integer :: tid

  !$omp parallel private(tid)
  tid = omp_get_thread_num()
  !$ print *, 'thread ', tid, ' of ', omp_get_num_threads()
  !$omp end parallel
end program demo

omp_master.title: omp_master
omp_master.name: omp_master
omp_master.summary: !$OMP MASTER - execute a block on the master thread only
omp_master.description:
**MASTER** has thread 0 execute the block. There is NO implicit barrier at
 either end, so the other threads run straight past.

 That is the trap: anything the master computed is not visible to the team
 without an explicit `barrier`. When the result is needed by everyone, `single`
 is almost always the construct meant.
omp_master.example_code:
!$omp master
  call write_checkpoint(step)
  !$omp end master
  !$omp barrier                  ! required -- master does not provide one

omp_nowait.title: nowait
omp_nowait.name: nowait
omp_nowait.summary: Remove the implicit barrier at the end of a worksharing construct
omp_nowait.description:
**nowait** removes the implicit barrier that otherwise ends a `do`, `single`
 or `sections` construct, letting a thread continue as soon as its own share
 is finished.

 It is a real optimization when the following code is independent, and a race
 when it is not: without the barrier there is no guarantee that other threads
 have written the results the next statement reads. That is the entire risk,
 and it is invisible in a small test where the loop finishes before anyone
 looks.

 A `parallel do` combined construct ends the parallel region, which always
 carries a barrier, so `nowait` does not apply there.
omp_nowait.example_code:
!$omp parallel
  !$omp do
  do i = 1, n
     a(i) = f(i)
  end do
  !$omp end do nowait            ! b does not depend on a
  !$omp do
  do i = 1, n
     b(i) = g(i)
  end do
  !$omp end do
  !$omp end parallel

omp_num_threads.title: num_threads(n)
omp_num_threads.name: num_threads(n)
omp_num_threads.summary: Request a thread count for this region only
omp_num_threads.description:
**num_threads** sets the team size for one region, overriding
 omp_set_num_threads and OMP_NUM_THREADS for that region alone.

 It is the surgical alternative to calling omp_set_num_threads, which changes
 the count for everything that follows -- including code the caller did not
 write. It is still only a request: dynamic adjustment can produce a smaller
 team unless omp_set_dynamic(.false.) is in force.
omp_num_threads.example_code:
!$omp parallel do num_threads(2)     ! this loop only
  do i = 1, n
     call io_bound_work(i)
  end do

omp_ordered.title: omp_ordered
omp_ordered.name: omp_ordered
omp_ordered.summary: !$OMP ORDERED - execute a loop body region in iteration order
omp_ordered.description:
**ORDERED** forces the enclosed region to execute in the sequential
 iteration order, while the rest of the loop body still runs in parallel. It
 exists mainly for output that must appear in order.

 The enclosing `do` needs the `ordered` clause, and each iteration may enter
 the region at most once. It serializes what it encloses, so keeping it small
 is the whole point.
omp_ordered.example_code:
!$omp parallel do ordered
  do i = 1, n
     call expensive(i, res)      ! parallel
     !$omp ordered
     write(10,*) i, res          ! in order
     !$omp end ordered
  end do

omp_parallel_do.title: omp_parallel_do
omp_parallel_do.name: omp_parallel_do

params.private(list): Creates a new private instance of each listed variable for each thread. The initial value is undefined. At the end of the parallel region, the original variable is unchanged.
params.shared(list): Specifies that listed variables are shared among all threads. All threads access the same storage location. Care must be taken to avoid race conditions.
params.default(none|shared|private): Sets the default data-sharing attribute for variables. Using `none` is recommended as it requires explicit specification of all variables, preventing accidental sharing bugs.
params.firstprivate(list): Like private, but each thread's copy is initialized from the original variable's value before the parallel region begins.
params.lastprivate(list): Like private, but the value from the sequentially last iteration is copied back to the original variable after the loop completes.
params.reduction(operator:list): Performs a reduction using the specified operator. Each thread has a private copy initialized appropriately (0 for +, 1 for *, etc.). At region end, partial results are combined. Operators: +, -, *, .and., .or., .eqv., .neqv., max, min, iand, ior, ieor.
params.schedule(type [, chunk_size]): Controls iteration distribution: - `static` - Iterations divided into chunks assigned round-robin (default) - `dynamic` - Threads take chunks from a queue as they finish - `guided` - Chunk sizes decrease exponentially - `runtime` - Determined by OMP_SCHEDULE environment variable - `auto` - Compiler/runtime decides
params.collapse(n): Combines n nested loops into one larger iteration space for better load balancing.
params.num_threads(expr): Specifies the number of threads for the parallel region.
params.if(expr): If false, the region executes serially with a single thread.

omp_parallel_do.description:
**!$omp parallel do** creates a parallel region containing a single worksharing-loop construct, distributing loop iterations across a team of threads. This combined construct is a shorthand for a parallel region containing only a single do directive, and is the most common OpenMP construct for parallelizing Fortran loops.

 When execution reaches the parallel do directive, a team of threads is created. The loop iterations are then distributed among the threads according to the schedule clause. Each thread executes its assigned portion of the loop iterations. At the end of the construct, threads synchronize at an implicit barrier before only the master thread continues.
omp_parallel_do.result: The parallel do construct distributes loop iterations across multiple threads, achieving parallel execution of the loop body. Upon completion, all threads have executed their assigned iterations, any reduction variables contain the combined result, and lastprivate variables hold the value from the final sequential iteration.
omp_parallel_do.example_code:
program demo_omp_parallel_do
  use omp_lib
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: n = 1000
  real(8) :: a(n), b(n), c(n)
  real(8) :: sum_result
  integer :: i, thread_id

  ! Initialize arrays
  do i = 1, n
    a(i) = real(i, 8)
    b(i) = real(i, 8) * 2.0d0
  end do

  ! Basic parallel do - array addition
  !$omp parallel do private(i) shared(a, b, c)
  do i = 1, n
    c(i) = a(i) + b(i)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do

  print '(A,F10.2)', 'c(1) = ', c(1)
  print '(A,F10.2)', 'c(n) = ', c(n)

  ! Parallel do with reduction
  sum_result = 0.0d0
  !$omp parallel do private(i) shared(a) reduction(+:sum_result)
  do i = 1, n
    sum_result = sum_result + a(i)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do

  print '(A,F15.2)', 'Sum of a: ', sum_result

  ! Parallel do with schedule and thread info
  !$omp parallel do private(i, thread_id) schedule(dynamic, 100)
  do i = 1, n
    thread_id = omp_get_thread_num()
    if (mod(i, 250) == 0) then
      !$omp critical
      print '(A,I4,A,I2)', 'Iteration ', i, ' executed by thread ', thread_id
      !$omp end critical
    end if
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do

end program demo_omp_parallel_do

omp_parallel_do_simd.title: omp_parallel_do_simd
omp_parallel_do_simd.name: omp_parallel_do_simd

params.private(list): Creates thread-private copies of listed variables. Within each thread, SIMD lanes may share or privatize these variables depending on the implementation.
params.shared(list): Specifies variables shared among all threads. Arrays accessed with the loop index are typically shared.
params.reduction(operator:list): Performs a reduction operation. The implementation combines both thread-level and SIMD-level reductions efficiently. Operators: +, -, *, .and., .or., .eqv., .neqv., max, min, iand, ior, ieor.
params.simdlen(length): Specifies the preferred number of SIMD lanes. Should match the hardware vector width for best performance (e.g., 4 for SSE with double, 8 for AVX with single).
params.safelen(length): Maximum number of iterations that can be executed concurrently without violating dependencies. If there are no loop-carried dependencies, this can be omitted.
params.aligned(list:alignment): Declares that array addresses are aligned to the specified byte boundary. Enables aligned vector load/store instructions. Common values: 16 (SSE), 32 (AVX), 64 (AVX-512).
params.linear(list:step): Specifies that listed variables have a linear relationship with the loop iteration, incrementing by step each iteration.
params.collapse(n): Combines n nested loops into a single iteration space before distributing and vectorizing.

omp_parallel_do_simd.description:
**!$omp parallel do simd** creates a parallel region containing a combined worksharing-loop and SIMD construct. Loop iterations are first distributed across threads, then each thread's iterations are vectorized using SIMD instructions. This provides two levels of parallelism: thread-level parallelism from the parallel do and data-level parallelism from SIMD vectorization.

 The loop body must be suitable for vectorization: no function calls (unless declared as simd), no I/O operations, no dependencies between SIMD lanes beyond what safelen allows, and operations should be uniform or linear.
omp_parallel_do_simd.result: The parallel do simd construct achieves both thread-level parallelism and SIMD vectorization. Loop iterations are distributed across threads, and each thread processes its iterations using vector instructions. Upon completion, any reduction variables contain the fully combined result from all threads and all SIMD lanes.
omp_parallel_do_simd.example_code:
program demo_omp_parallel_do_simd
  use omp_lib
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: n = 10000
  real(8), allocatable :: a(:), b(:), c(:)
  real(8) :: sum_val, dot_product_val
  integer :: i

  allocate(a(n), b(n), c(n))

  ! Initialize arrays
  do i = 1, n
    a(i) = real(i, 8) * 0.001d0
    b(i) = real(n - i + 1, 8) * 0.001d0
  end do

  ! Parallel do simd: array addition with SIMD vectorization
  !$omp parallel do simd private(i) shared(a, b, c) simdlen(8)
  do i = 1, n
    c(i) = a(i) + b(i)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do simd

  print '(A,F12.6)', 'c(1)   = ', c(1)
  print '(A,F12.6)', 'c(n)   = ', c(n)
  print '(A,F12.6)', 'c(n/2) = ', c(n/2)

  ! Parallel do simd with reduction: sum
  sum_val = 0.0d0
  !$omp parallel do simd private(i) reduction(+:sum_val)
  do i = 1, n
    sum_val = sum_val + c(i)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do simd

  print '(A,F15.6)', 'Sum of c: ', sum_val

  ! Parallel do simd: dot product
  dot_product_val = 0.0d0
  !$omp parallel do simd private(i) reduction(+:dot_product_val)
  do i = 1, n
    dot_product_val = dot_product_val + a(i) * b(i)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do simd

  print '(A,F15.6)', 'Dot product a.b: ', dot_product_val

  deallocate(a, b, c)

end program demo_omp_parallel_do_simd

omp_private.title: private(list)
omp_private.name: private(list)
omp_private.summary: Give each thread its own uninitialized copy of each variable
omp_private.description:
**private** gives every thread its own copy of each listed variable.

 The copies are UNINITIALIZED on entry -- they do not inherit the value the
 variable had outside the region. Code that reads a private variable before
 assigning it reads garbage, and because the original often still happens to
 be in the register or on the stack, it frequently appears to work in testing
 and fails under load. When the incoming value is needed, the clause wanted is
 `firstprivate`.

 The value is also DISCARDED at the end of the region: the original variable
 is unchanged. Use `lastprivate` to keep the sequentially-last iteration's
 value.

 Loop control variables of a parallelized `do` are private automatically;
 anything else used as scratch inside the loop is not, and a shared scratch
 variable is the most common OpenMP race.
omp_private.example_code:
!$omp parallel do private(j, tmp)
  do i = 1, n
     tmp = 0.0d0                  ! MUST assign before reading
     do j = 1, m
        tmp = tmp + a(i,j)
     end do
     rowsum(i) = tmp
  end do

omp_reduction.title: omp_reduction
omp_reduction.name: omp_reduction
omp_reduction.summary: Reduction clause for parallel accumulation operations

params.+ (addition): Identity value: 0. Combines partial sums from all threads.
params.- (subtraction): Identity value: 0. Note: Subtraction is not truly associative; treated as addition of negated values.
params.* (multiplication): Identity value: 1. Combines partial products from all threads.
params..and. (logical AND): Identity value: .true.. Result is .true. only if all partial results are .true..
params..or. (logical OR): Identity value: .false.. Result is .true. if any partial result is .true..
params..eqv. (logical equivalence): Identity value: .true.. Tests if all partial results have the same logical value.
params..neqv. (logical non-equivalence): Identity value: .false.. Logical XOR across all threads.
params.max (maximum): Identity value: smallest representable value for the type. Finds maximum across all threads.
params.min (minimum): Identity value: largest representable value for the type. Finds minimum across all threads.
params.iand (bitwise AND): Identity value: all bits set to 1. Performs bitwise AND across all threads.
params.ior (bitwise OR): Identity value: 0. Performs bitwise OR across all threads.
params.ieor (bitwise XOR): Identity value: 0. Performs bitwise XOR across all threads.

omp_reduction.description:
**reduction(operator:list)** is a data-sharing clause that enables safe parallel accumulation of values into shared variables. Without reduction, multiple threads updating the same variable would cause a race condition. With reduction, each thread accumulates into its own private copy, and these copies are combined at the end of the parallel region.

 The private copies are initialized to the identity value for the operator: 0 for +, 1 for *, .true. for .and., .false. for .or., largest negative for max, largest positive for min, all bits set for iand, and zero for ior and ieor.
omp_reduction.result: After the parallel region completes, the reduction variable contains the combined result of the reduction operation applied across all threads. The order of combination is implementation-defined but mathematically equivalent to sequential execution for associative operators.
omp_reduction.example_code:
program demo_omp_reduction
  use omp_lib
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: n = 10000
  real(8) :: a(n)
  real(8) :: sum_val, product_val, max_val, min_val
  integer :: count_positive
  logical :: all_positive, any_negative
  integer :: i

  ! Initialize array with mixed values
  do i = 1, n
    a(i) = real(i - n/2, 8)  ! Values from -5000 to 5000
  end do

  ! Reduction with + (sum)
  sum_val = 0.0d0
  !$omp parallel do reduction(+:sum_val)
  do i = 1, n
    sum_val = sum_val + a(i)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do
  print '(A,F15.2)', 'Sum:     ', sum_val

  ! Reduction with max
  max_val = -huge(max_val)
  !$omp parallel do reduction(max:max_val)
  do i = 1, n
    max_val = max(max_val, a(i))
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do
  print '(A,F15.2)', 'Maximum: ', max_val

  ! Reduction with min
  min_val = huge(min_val)
  !$omp parallel do reduction(min:min_val)
  do i = 1, n
    min_val = min(min_val, a(i))
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do
  print '(A,F15.2)', 'Minimum: ', min_val

  ! Logical reduction: .and.
  all_positive = .true.
  !$omp parallel do reduction(.and.:all_positive)
  do i = 1, n
    all_positive = all_positive .and. (a(i) > 0.0d0)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do
  print '(A,L)', 'All positive: ', all_positive

  ! Logical reduction: .or.
  any_negative = .false.
  !$omp parallel do reduction(.or.:any_negative)
  do i = 1, n
    any_negative = any_negative .or. (a(i) < 0.0d0)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do
  print '(A,L)', 'Any negative: ', any_negative

  ! Integer reduction: count
  count_positive = 0
  !$omp parallel do reduction(+:count_positive)
  do i = 1, n
    if (a(i) > 0.0d0) count_positive = count_positive + 1
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do
  print '(A,I0)', 'Count positive: ', count_positive

  ! Multiple reductions in one directive
  sum_val = 0.0d0
  max_val = -huge(max_val)
  min_val = huge(min_val)
  !$omp parallel do reduction(+:sum_val) reduction(max:max_val) reduction(min:min_val)
  do i = 1, n
    sum_val = sum_val + a(i)
    max_val = max(max_val, a(i))
    min_val = min(min_val, a(i))
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do
  print '(A)', 'Combined reductions:'
  print '(A,F15.2)', '  Sum: ', sum_val
  print '(A,F15.2)', '  Max: ', max_val
  print '(A,F15.2)', '  Min: ', min_val

end program demo_omp_reduction
omp_reduction.standard: OpenMP 1.0 (1997 for Fortran), with extensions in later versions

omp_schedule.title: schedule(kind[, chunk])
omp_schedule.name: schedule(kind[, chunk])
omp_schedule.summary: Choose how loop iterations are distributed across threads
omp_schedule.description:
**schedule** selects how iterations are handed to threads.

 `static` splits them into equal contiguous chunks up front: no run-time
 overhead, and the right choice when every iteration costs about the same. It
 is also the only kind guaranteed to give the same mapping across two loops
 with matching bounds, which matters when one loop's output is read by
 position in the next.

 `dynamic` hands out chunks on demand, which balances irregular work at the
 cost of synchronization per chunk -- a chunk size of 1 on a cheap loop body
 is usually slower than static. `guided` starts with large chunks and shrinks
 them. `runtime` defers the decision to OMP_SCHEDULE or omp_set_schedule.

 With a neighbour-list or cutoff-based loop -- where the work per iteration
 varies by an order of magnitude -- `dynamic` with a chunk of a few dozen is
 usually the right starting point.
omp_schedule.example_code:
! Cost per atom varies with neighbour count
  !$omp parallel do schedule(dynamic, 32) reduction(+:etot)
  do i = 1, natoms
     etot = etot + pair_energy(i)
  end do

omp_section.title: !$OMP SECTION
omp_section.name: !$OMP SECTION
omp_section.summary: Mark one block within a SECTIONS construct
omp_section.description:
**SECTION** delimits one unit of work inside a `sections` construct. Each is
 executed once, by one thread; which thread is unspecified.

 It is valid only lexically inside `sections`.
omp_section.example_code:
!$omp sections
  !$omp section
  call phase_a()
  !$omp section
  call phase_b()
  !$omp end sections

omp_sections.title: !$OMP SECTIONS
omp_sections.name: !$OMP SECTIONS
omp_sections.summary: Distribute distinct blocks of code across threads
omp_sections.description:
**SECTIONS** assigns different blocks of code -- rather than different
 iterations -- to different threads. It expresses functional parallelism: two
 independent routines that can run at the same time.

 It scales only as far as the number of sections written, so it does not
 benefit from a larger machine. Where the work can be expressed as a loop or
 as tasks, those scale and this does not.

 There is an implicit barrier at the end unless `nowait` is given.
omp_sections.example_code:
!$omp parallel
  !$omp sections
  !$omp section
  call compute_forces()
  !$omp section
  call update_neighbour_list()
  !$omp end sections
  !$omp end parallel

omp_set_dynamic.title: omp_set_dynamic
omp_set_dynamic.name: omp_set_dynamic
omp_set_dynamic.summary: Enable or disable dynamic adjustment of thread counts

params.dynamic_threads: LOGICAL; .TRUE. permits the runtime to reduce team sizes.

omp_set_dynamic.description:
**omp_set_dynamic** controls whether the runtime may choose a team size
 smaller than requested. With it enabled -- the default in several
 implementations -- a parallel region can start with fewer threads than
 omp_get_max_threads() reported.

 Disable it when correctness depends on the exact count, which is the case for
 any code indexing a per-thread array sized in advance.
omp_set_dynamic.result: Dynamic adjustment is enabled or disabled for later regions.
omp_set_dynamic.example_code:
call omp_set_dynamic(.false.)      ! I want exactly what I ask for
  call omp_set_num_threads(8)

omp_set_lock.title: omp_set_lock
omp_set_lock.name: omp_set_lock
omp_set_lock.summary: Acquire an OpenMP lock, blocking until it is available
omp_set_lock.description:
**omp_set_lock** blocks until the lock is available and then acquires it.
 The lock must have been initialized by omp_init_lock.

 Locks are the general but blunt tool. A `critical` or `atomic` construct
 expresses most mutual exclusion more clearly and lets the compiler do better;
 reach for locks when the region to protect is chosen at run time -- a
 per-element lock array, for instance. A thread that takes a simple lock it
 already holds deadlocks; use a nestable lock for that.
omp_set_lock.result: The lock is held by the calling thread on return.
omp_set_lock.example_code:
integer(kind=omp_lock_kind) :: lck
  call omp_init_lock(lck)
  !$omp parallel
  call omp_set_lock(lck)
  total = total + local
  call omp_unset_lock(lck)
  !$omp end parallel
  call omp_destroy_lock(lck)

omp_set_max_active_levels.title: omp_set_max_active_levels
omp_set_max_active_levels.name: omp_set_max_active_levels
omp_set_max_active_levels.summary: Set the maximum depth of active nested parallelism

params.max_levels: Maximum depth of active nested regions.

omp_set_max_active_levels.description:
**omp_set_max_active_levels** limits how deeply active parallel regions may
 nest. Beyond the limit, inner regions still execute but with a single thread.

 The default of 1 is why an inner parallel region often appears to be ignored:
 nesting is disabled, not broken.
omp_set_max_active_levels.example_code: call omp_set_max_active_levels(2)   ! allow one level of nesting

omp_set_nest_lock.title: omp_set_nest_lock
omp_set_nest_lock.name: omp_set_nest_lock
omp_set_nest_lock.description:
**omp_set_nest_lock** acquires a nestable lock, incrementing its count when
 the calling thread already holds it. It must be released once per acquisition.
omp_set_nest_lock.result: The lock is held; its nesting count is incremented.

omp_set_nested.title: omp_set_nested
omp_set_nested.name: omp_set_nested
omp_set_nested.description:
**omp_set_nested** enables or disables nested parallel regions.

 Deprecated in OpenMP 5.0 in favour of omp_set_max_active_levels, which says
 the same thing precisely -- `omp_set_nested(.true.)` means only "more than one
 level", without saying how many.
omp_set_nested.result: Nested parallelism is enabled or disabled.
omp_set_nested.example_code:
call omp_set_max_active_levels(2)   ! preferred
  ! call omp_set_nested(.true.)       ! deprecated

omp_set_num_threads.title: omp_set_num_threads
omp_set_num_threads.name: omp_set_num_threads
omp_set_num_threads.summary: Set the thread count for subsequent parallel regions

params.num_threads: Number of threads to request; must be positive.

omp_set_num_threads.description:
**omp_set_num_threads** sets how many threads later parallel regions
 request. It affects regions started AFTER the call and never the one
 currently executing, and it must be called from serial code.

 It overrides the OMP_NUM_THREADS environment variable, which is usually the
 wrong thing for a batch job -- hard-coding a count here ignores what the
 scheduler allocated. A num_threads clause on a single region is the more
 surgical tool.
omp_set_num_threads.example_code:
call omp_set_num_threads(4)
  !$omp parallel            ! 4 threads
  !$omp end parallel

omp_set_schedule.title: omp_set_schedule
omp_set_schedule.name: omp_set_schedule
omp_set_schedule.summary: Set the schedule used by `schedule(runtime)` loops

params.chunk_size: Chunk size; the implementation's default is used when it is not positive.

omp_set_schedule.description:
**omp_set_schedule** sets the schedule that loops marked
 `schedule(runtime)` will use, overriding OMP_SCHEDULE. It lets a program pick
 a schedule from its own measurements rather than at compile time.

 Kinds are omp_sched_static, omp_sched_dynamic, omp_sched_guided and
 omp_sched_auto.
omp_set_schedule.result: Later `schedule(runtime)` loops use the given schedule.
omp_set_schedule.example_code:
call omp_set_schedule(omp_sched_dynamic, 16)
  !$omp parallel do schedule(runtime)
  do i = 1, n
     call variable_cost_work(i)
  end do

omp_shared.title: shared(list)
omp_shared.name: shared(list)
omp_shared.summary: Share one copy of each variable across the whole team
omp_shared.description:
**shared** declares that all threads refer to the same storage. It is the
 default for most variables in a parallel region, which is precisely why races
 are easy to write: a variable that should have been scratch is shared unless
 something says otherwise.

 OpenMP provides no synchronization for shared data. Concurrent writes, or a
 read racing a write, need `atomic`, `critical`, a `reduction` clause or a
 lock. Reading a shared variable that nobody writes is always safe.

 `default(none)` forces every variable to be classified explicitly and is the
 single most effective way to find these bugs.
omp_shared.example_code:
!$omp parallel do default(none) shared(a, n) private(i)
  do i = 1, n
     a(i) = 2.0d0 * a(i)          ! disjoint elements -- safe
  end do

omp_simd.title: !$OMP SIMD
omp_simd.name: !$OMP SIMD
omp_simd.summary: Vectorize a loop across SIMD lanes
omp_simd.description:
**SIMD** asks the compiler to execute loop iterations concurrently in vector
 lanes. It is orthogonal to threading: `simd` alone uses no threads, and
 `parallel do simd` does both.

 It is an assertion, not a request. The directive tells the compiler the
 iterations are independent, so it may vectorize without proving it -- and if
 they are not independent, the result is wrong with no diagnostic. A loop
 carrying a dependence must not be marked.

 Compilers auto-vectorize much of this already; the directive earns its place
 where a dependence cannot be disproved automatically.
omp_simd.example_code:
!$omp parallel do simd reduction(+:s)
  do i = 1, n
     s = s + a(i) * b(i)
  end do

omp_single.title: omp_single
omp_single.name: omp_single
omp_single.summary: !$OMP SINGLE - execute a block on exactly one thread
omp_single.description:
**SINGLE** has one -- unspecified -- thread execute the block while the
 others wait at the implicit barrier at its end. `nowait` removes that
 barrier.

 It differs from `master` in two ways that matter: the thread is not
 necessarily thread 0, and `master` has NO implicit barrier. Code that uses
 `master` and assumes synchronization afterwards is racing.
omp_single.example_code:
!$omp parallel
  !$omp single
  call read_input(params)        ! once, and everyone waits
  !$omp end single
  call use(params)               ! safe: barrier has passed
  !$omp end parallel

omp_task.title: omp_task
omp_task.name: omp_task
omp_task.summary: !$OMP TASK - create an explicit unit of deferred work
omp_task.description:
**TASK** packages a block as a unit of work that any thread in the team may
 run, at any time up to the next task barrier. It is how recursion and linked
 structures are parallelized, where a counted `do` loop cannot express the work.

 The critical detail is variable scoping: task variables default to
 `firstprivate`, not `shared`, and a task can outlive the scope that created
 it -- so a task referring to a loop variable by `shared` usually reads the
 wrong value by the time it runs.

 Completion is guaranteed only at a `taskwait` or a barrier.
omp_task.example_code:
!$omp parallel
  !$omp single
  call traverse(root)            ! one thread seeds the work
  !$omp end single
  !$omp end parallel

  recursive subroutine traverse(node)
     !$omp task firstprivate(node)
     call visit(node)
     !$omp end task
     if (associated(node%next)) call traverse(node%next)
  end subroutine

omp_taskgroup.title: !$OMP TASKGROUP
omp_taskgroup.name: !$OMP TASKGROUP
omp_taskgroup.summary: Wait for a set of tasks and all their descendants
omp_taskgroup.description:
**TASKGROUP** waits, at its end, for every task created inside it AND all of
 their descendants.

 That is the difference from `taskwait`, which waits only for the current
 task's immediate children. Recursive task decomposition needs a taskgroup;
 a taskwait there returns while grandchildren are still running.
omp_taskgroup.example_code:
!$omp taskgroup
  call recursive_traverse(root)   ! creates tasks that create tasks
  !$omp end taskgroup             ! all of them are done here

omp_taskwait.title: omp_taskwait
omp_taskwait.name: omp_taskwait
omp_taskwait.summary: !$OMP TASKWAIT - wait for the current task's child tasks
omp_taskwait.description:
**TASKWAIT** blocks until the tasks generated directly by the current task
 have completed. It waits for CHILDREN only, not for their descendants -- use
 `taskgroup` for the whole subtree.
omp_taskwait.example_code:
!$omp task
  call left_half()
  !$omp end task
  call right_half()
  !$omp taskwait                 ! left_half is now done
  call combine()

omp_test_lock.title: omp_test_lock
omp_test_lock.name: omp_test_lock
omp_test_lock.summary: Try to acquire a lock without blocking
omp_test_lock.description:
**omp_test_lock** attempts to acquire the lock and returns immediately,
 reporting whether it succeeded. It lets a thread do something else instead of
 waiting -- the basis of a work-stealing loop.

 The lock is held only when the result is .TRUE., and only then must it be
 released.
omp_test_lock.result: .TRUE. if the lock was acquired, .FALSE. otherwise.
omp_test_lock.example_code:
if (omp_test_lock(lck)) then
     call flush_shared_buffer()
     call omp_unset_lock(lck)
  else
     call do_local_work()
  end if

omp_test_nest_lock.title: omp_test_nest_lock
omp_test_nest_lock.name: omp_test_nest_lock
omp_test_nest_lock.summary: Try to acquire a nestable lock without blocking

params.nvar: The nestable lock variable to try.

omp_test_nest_lock.description:
**omp_test_nest_lock** attempts to acquire a nestable lock and returns
 immediately. Note the return type: it is the new nesting count, an INTEGER,
 and zero means the attempt failed -- unlike omp_test_lock, which returns a
 LOGICAL.
omp_test_nest_lock.result: The new nesting count, or 0 if the lock could not be acquired.
omp_test_nest_lock.example_code:
if (omp_test_nest_lock(nlck) > 0) then
     call work()
     call omp_unset_nest_lock(nlck)
  end if

omp_threadprivate.title: omp_threadprivate
omp_threadprivate.name: omp_threadprivate
omp_threadprivate.summary: !$OMP THREADPRIVATE - give each thread its own copy of a variable
omp_threadprivate.description:
**THREADPRIVATE** gives each thread a private copy of a named COMMON block
 or SAVEd variable, persisting across parallel regions.

 It is the tool for threading legacy Fortran, where working state lives in
 COMMON: without it, every thread shares one copy and the results are
 nondeterministic garbage. The directive must follow the declaration, and
 appear in every scoping unit that declares the block.

 Copies other than the master's are undefined on entry to the first region
 unless `copyin` initializes them.
omp_threadprivate.example_code:
common /work/ scratch(1000)
  !$omp threadprivate(/work/)

  !$omp parallel copyin(/work/)
  call uses_scratch()            ! each thread has its own
  !$omp end parallel

omp_unset_lock.title: omp_unset_lock
omp_unset_lock.name: omp_unset_lock

params.svar: The lock variable, currently held by this thread.

omp_unset_lock.description:
**omp_unset_lock** releases a lock held by the calling thread. Releasing a
 lock the thread does not hold is undefined.

 Every path out of the protected region must release it -- including error
 paths and any Fortran RETURN, which is the usual way a lock is leaked.

omp_unset_nest_lock.title: omp_unset_nest_lock
omp_unset_nest_lock.name: omp_unset_nest_lock
omp_unset_nest_lock.description:
**omp_unset_nest_lock** decrements the lock's nesting count, releasing it
 to other threads only when the count reaches zero.
omp_unset_nest_lock.result: The nesting count is decremented; the lock frees at zero.

omp_workshare.title: !$OMP WORKSHARE
omp_workshare.name: !$OMP WORKSHARE
omp_workshare.summary: Divide the work of Fortran array statements across threads
omp_workshare.description:
**WORKSHARE** is Fortran-only: it splits the work of array assignments,
 `FORALL`, `WHERE` and array intrinsics such as `SUM` and `MATMUL` across the
 team. It is the natural way to parallelize array-syntax code without
 rewriting it as explicit loops.

 Statements inside are executed as if in sequential order, so it is safe but
 also limited -- and implementations vary considerably in how much
 parallelism they actually extract. Explicit loops with `do` are more
 predictable.
omp_workshare.example_code:
!$omp parallel
  !$omp workshare
  temp = temp + dt * flux
  !$omp end workshare
  !$omp end parallel

ompatomic.title: omp_atomic
ompatomic.name: omp_atomic
ompatomic.summary: Atomic memory operation for thread-safe updates

params.read: Atomically reads the value of x into v. Syntax: `v = x`
params.write: Atomically writes the value of expr to x. Syntax: `x = expr`
params.update** (default)\n : Atomically updat: Atomically updates x and captures either the original or final value. Requires `!$omp end atomic`. Syntax: `v = x; x = x op expr` or `v = x; x = expr; !$omp end atomic`
params.seq_cst: Sequentially consistent memory ordering. Provides the strongest ordering guarantees.
params.acq_rel: Acquire-release memory ordering for capture operations.
params.release: Release memory ordering for write and update operations.
params.acquire: Acquire memory ordering for read operations.
params.relaxed: Relaxed memory ordering. No synchronization with other operations.
params.hint(hint-expression): OpenMP 5.0+ hint about contention (uncontended, contended, nonspeculative, speculative).

ompatomic.description:
**!$omp atomic** ensures that a specific storage location is accessed atomically, preventing data races when multiple threads update shared variables. The atomic construct provides a lightweight synchronization mechanism compared to critical sections, often with hardware support on modern processors.

 The default behavior (without a clause) is atomic update, which performs a read-modify-write operation atomically. The read, write, and capture clauses provide additional atomic operations for different use cases.
ompatomic.result: The atomic construct ensures that the specified memory operation on x completes without interference from other threads. For update operations, the final value of x reflects the atomic combination of all thread updates. For capture operations, v contains the captured value as specified.
ompatomic.example_code:
program demo_omp_atomic
  use omp_lib
  implicit none
  integer :: counter, max_val, min_val
  integer :: captured_before, captured_after
  real(8) :: sum_val
  integer :: i
  integer, parameter :: n = 1000

  ! Example 1: Atomic update (increment counter)
  counter = 0
  !$omp parallel do
  do i = 1, n
    !$omp atomic update
    counter = counter + 1
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do
  print '(A,I0)', 'Counter (should be 1000): ', counter

  ! Example 2: Atomic with max
  max_val = 0
  !$omp parallel do private(i)
  do i = 1, n
    !$omp atomic update
    max_val = max(max_val, i)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do
  print '(A,I0)', 'Maximum value: ', max_val

  ! Example 3: Atomic with min
  min_val = huge(min_val)
  !$omp parallel do private(i)
  do i = 1, n
    !$omp atomic update
    min_val = min(min_val, i)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do
  print '(A,I0)', 'Minimum value: ', min_val

  ! Example 4: Atomic update with real
  sum_val = 0.0d0
  !$omp parallel do private(i)
  do i = 1, n
    !$omp atomic update
    sum_val = sum_val + real(i, 8)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do
  print '(A,F12.2)', 'Sum (should be 500500.0): ', sum_val

  ! Example 5: Atomic read
  counter = 42
  !$omp parallel
  !$omp single
    !$omp atomic read
    captured_before = counter
    print '(A,I0)', 'Captured value: ', captured_before
  !$omp end single
  !$omp end parallel

  ! Example 6: Atomic write
  !$omp parallel
  !$omp single
    !$omp atomic write
    counter = 100
  !$omp end single
  !$omp end parallel
  print '(A,I0)', 'Counter after atomic write: ', counter

  ! Example 7: Atomic capture
  counter = 0
  !$omp parallel do private(i, captured_before)
  do i = 1, 10
    !$omp atomic capture
    captured_before = counter
    counter = counter + 1
    !$omp end atomic
    !$omp critical
    print '(A,I2,A,I2,A,I2)', 'Thread got ', captured_before, &
          ', incremented to ', captured_before + 1, ' at iteration ', i
    !$omp end critical
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do
  print '(A,I0)', 'Final counter: ', counter

end program demo_omp_atomic
ompatomic.standard: OpenMP 1.0 (basic atomic), OpenMP 3.1 (read/write/capture), OpenMP 4.5 (seq_cst), OpenMP 5.0 (memory order clauses)

ompbarrier.title: barrier
ompbarrier.name: barrier
ompbarrier.description:
**barrier** specifies an explicit synchronization point at which all threads in the current team must wait. When a thread reaches the barrier directive, it halts execution until all other threads in the team have also reached the barrier. Once all threads arrive and complete any pending explicit tasks bound to the parallel region, they resume parallel execution of subsequent code.

 The barrier construct ensures that all work performed by threads before the barrier is visible to all threads after the barrier. This is essential for maintaining data consistency when threads need to share results from parallel computations.

### **Options**\n\nNone. This is a stand-alone synchronization construct that accepts no clauses or arguments.
ompbarrier.result: When all threads have reached the barrier, the synchronization is complete. All memory operations performed before the barrier by any thread are guaranteed to be visible to all threads after the barrier. Execution resumes with all threads synchronized at the same point in the program. The barrier establishes a happens-before relationship between code preceding and following the barrier across all threads.
ompbarrier.example_code:
program demo_omp_barrier
  use omp_lib
  implicit none
  integer :: thread_id
  integer, parameter :: n = 4
  integer :: partial_sums(n)
  integer :: total_sum
  integer :: i

  total_sum = 0

  !$omp parallel num_threads(n) private(thread_id) shared(partial_sums, total_sum)
    thread_id = omp_get_thread_num()

    ! Each thread computes its partial sum
    partial_sums(thread_id + 1) = (thread_id + 1) * 10
    print '(A,I0,A,I0)', 'Thread ', thread_id, ' computed partial sum: ', partial_sums(thread_id + 1)

    ! Wait for all threads to finish computing
    !$omp barrier

    ! Only thread 0 computes the total after all partial sums are ready
    !$omp single
      do i = 1, n
        total_sum = total_sum + partial_sums(i)
      end do
      print '(A,I0)', 'Total sum after barrier: ', total_sum
    !$omp end single
  !$omp end parallel

end program demo_omp_barrier

ompcritical.title: critical
ompcritical.name: critical

params.name: Optional identifier for the critical region. Names are global entities of the program in Fortran. Critical regions with the same name share mutual exclusion. If omitted, the critical section shares an implicit common name with all other unnamed critical sections.
params.hint(hint-expression): Optional clause providing implementation hints about expected runtime properties. Valid hint values (from `omp_lib` module): - `omp_sync_hint_none` (default) - No hint specified - `omp_sync_hint_uncontended` - Low contention expected - `omp_sync_hint_contended` - High contention expected - `omp_sync_hint_nonspeculative` - Use non-speculative locking - `omp_sync_hint_speculative` - Use speculative locking (hardware transactional memory) Hints do not affect isolation guarantees and may be ignored by the implementation. A hint clause requires a named construct.

ompcritical.description:
**critical** restricts execution of the associated structured block to a single thread at a time. When a thread encounters a critical region, it waits until no other thread in the contention group is executing that named critical region. This provides mutual exclusion synchronization for the enclosed code block.

 The optional name acts as a global identifier. Different critical regions with the same name enforce mutual exclusion against each other across all threads in the contention group, regardless of which team the threads belong to.
ompcritical.result: The critical construct ensures that only one thread at a time executes the enclosed structured block. Upon exiting the critical region, the thread releases the lock, allowing another waiting thread to enter. All memory operations within the critical region are protected from concurrent access by other threads entering the same named (or unnamed) critical region.
ompcritical.example_code:
program demo_omp_critical
  use omp_lib
  implicit none
  integer :: total, thread_id
  integer :: i
  integer, parameter :: n = 100

  total = 0

  !$omp parallel private(thread_id, i)
    thread_id = omp_get_thread_num()

    ! Named critical section for safe accumulation
    do i = 1, n
      !$omp critical (accumulate)
        total = total + 1
      !$omp end critical (accumulate)
    end do

    ! Unnamed critical for I/O
    !$omp critical
      print '(A,I2,A,I6)', 'Thread ', thread_id, ' sees total = ', total
    !$omp end critical

  !$omp end parallel

  print '(A,I6)', 'Final total = ', total

end program demo_omp_critical

ompdo.title: omp_parallel_do
ompdo.name: omp_parallel_do

params.private(list): Creates a new private instance of each listed variable for each thread. The initial value is undefined. At the end of the parallel region, the original variable is unchanged.
params.shared(list): Specifies that listed variables are shared among all threads. All threads access the same storage location. Care must be taken to avoid race conditions.
params.default(none|shared|private): Sets the default data-sharing attribute for variables. Using `none` is recommended as it requires explicit specification of all variables, preventing accidental sharing bugs.
params.firstprivate(list): Like private, but each thread's copy is initialized from the original variable's value before the parallel region begins.
params.lastprivate(list): Like private, but the value from the sequentially last iteration is copied back to the original variable after the loop completes.
params.reduction(operator:list): Performs a reduction using the specified operator. Each thread has a private copy initialized appropriately (0 for +, 1 for *, etc.). At region end, partial results are combined. Operators: +, -, *, .and., .or., .eqv., .neqv., max, min, iand, ior, ieor.
params.schedule(type [, chunk_size]): Controls iteration distribution: - `static` - Iterations divided into chunks assigned round-robin (default) - `dynamic` - Threads take chunks from a queue as they finish - `guided` - Chunk sizes decrease exponentially - `runtime` - Determined by OMP_SCHEDULE environment variable - `auto` - Compiler/runtime decides
params.collapse(n): Combines n nested loops into one larger iteration space for better load balancing.
params.num_threads(expr): Specifies the number of threads for the parallel region.
params.if(expr): If false, the region executes serially with a single thread.

ompdo.description:
**!$omp parallel do** creates a parallel region containing a single worksharing-loop construct, distributing loop iterations across a team of threads. This combined construct is a shorthand for a parallel region containing only a single do directive, and is the most common OpenMP construct for parallelizing Fortran loops.

 When execution reaches the parallel do directive, a team of threads is created. The loop iterations are then distributed among the threads according to the schedule clause. Each thread executes its assigned portion of the loop iterations. At the end of the construct, threads synchronize at an implicit barrier before only the master thread continues.
ompdo.result: The parallel do construct distributes loop iterations across multiple threads, achieving parallel execution of the loop body. Upon completion, all threads have executed their assigned iterations, any reduction variables contain the combined result, and lastprivate variables hold the value from the final sequential iteration.
ompdo.example_code:
program demo_omp_parallel_do
  use omp_lib
  implicit none
  integer, parameter :: n = 1000
  real(8) :: a(n), b(n), c(n)
  real(8) :: sum_result
  integer :: i, thread_id

  ! Initialize arrays
  do i = 1, n
    a(i) = real(i, 8)
    b(i) = real(i, 8) * 2.0d0
  end do

  ! Basic parallel do - array addition
  !$omp parallel do private(i) shared(a, b, c)
  do i = 1, n
    c(i) = a(i) + b(i)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do

  print '(A,F10.2)', 'c(1) = ', c(1)
  print '(A,F10.2)', 'c(n) = ', c(n)

  ! Parallel do with reduction
  sum_result = 0.0d0
  !$omp parallel do private(i) shared(a) reduction(+:sum_result)
  do i = 1, n
    sum_result = sum_result + a(i)
  end do
  !$omp end parallel do

  print '(A,F15.2)', 'Sum of a: ', sum_result

  ! Parallel do with schedule and thread info
  !$omp parallel do private(i, thread_id) schedule(dynamic, 100)
  do i = 1, n
    thread_id = omp_get_thread_num()
    if (mod(i, 250) == 0) then
      !$omp critical
